Switch to any available commercial application without checking authorization
Wait for orders to create an alternate arrangement after the failure
questions.explanation: Redundancy and PACE planning prepare recovery arrangements before disruption. When the primary link fails, personnel already know the authorized alternate, use it to keep communicating, and coordinate repair of the primary.
why: Stopping communication defeats the purpose of a pre-established alternate.
An unauthorized commercial application may not meet COMSEC requirements.
The alternate was already established beforehand; waiting to create one wastes the preparation.

questions.stem: How should limited signal resources be prioritized?
questions.key: By supportability and importance to mission accomplishment
distractors: By equipment age and the order in which requests arrive
By the rank of the requesting unit's commander
Equally among all units regardless of their mission
questions.explanation: When requirements exceed capability, planners compare requirements with resources and set priorities by supportability and importance to mission accomplishment, consistent with the commander's guidance and intent.
why: Equipment age and arrival order are not mission-based criteria.
Rank does not determine mission importance or supportability.
Equal sharing ignores mission importance and may starve critical requirements.

questions.stem: An Army unit ashore receives delayed messages from a supporting naval element because their systems cannot communicate directly. What is the best signal support action?
questions.key: Coordinate compatible equipment or an approved embedded-operator relay arrangement
distractors: Wait for the naval element to replace its systems with Army equipment
Send the traffic over unprotected commercial applications
Stop exchanging messages until the operation ends
questions.explanation: Joint signal support bridges gaps between services through compatible equipment and coordinated radio operators. An Army operator embedded with the naval element can relay information between troops ashore and the naval support.
why: Waiting for a wholesale equipment replacement is impractical and leaves the delay unresolved.
Unprotected commercial applications do not satisfy COMSEC requirements for operational traffic.
Stopping the exchange removes the coordination the joint force needs.

questions.stem: A commander may need timely information, but speed does not remove the requirement to use an appropriately protected communication method. During a coalition operation, which key component of signal support is primarily highlighted by balancing the need for speed with the mandate for protection?
questions.explanation: Secure communication means protecting information from unauthorized access, interception or manipulation. A commander's need for speed does not remove the requirement to use an appropriately protected method.
why: Interoperability is about systems and procedures working together, not about protecting information.
Scalable systems is about adjusting to growth in size, location and tempo.
Technical support and maintenance is about equipment readiness, troubleshooting and restoration.

questions.stem: During a combined arms operation, the Signal Officer evaluates which maneuver elements and supporting arms must communicate, the critical data they must exchange, and the systems required to link them together. Which pillar of the Philippine Army Signal Operations Framework is being applied?
questions.explanation: Connect is the pillar of establishing connectivity among units. Deciding which maneuver elements and supporting arms must communicate, what data they exchange and which systems link them is applying Connect.
why: Sustain keeps connectivity going through personnel, power and maintenance, not deciding who must be linked.
Recover repairs and restores communication after disruption.
Redundant is one of the five principles of signal operations, not a pillar of the framework.

questions.stem: A joint network operator detects suspicious activity affecting Army and Navy systems. What is the most appropriate action?
questions.key: Report through established channels and activate coordinated incident-response procedures
distractors: Disconnect all Army and Navy systems permanently and delete the logs
Investigate and repair it alone without informing anyone
Ignore the activity until it affects mission traffic
questions.explanation: Suspicious activity is reported through established procedures, and designated incident responders investigate and direct corrective action. In joint operations the Army and Navy responses are coordinated.
why: Permanent disconnection and deleting logs destroys evidence and the joint capability.
Acting alone bypasses the responders who investigate the extent of compromise.
Waiting allows a possible compromise to spread unreported.

questions.stem: Different terminology, procedures, and communication habits can create misunderstanding even when systems are technically compatible. Which challenge to coalition signal support does this describe?
questions.explanation: Even when systems are technically compatible, different terminology, procedures and communication habits can cause misunderstanding. This is the language and cultural barriers challenge.
why: Technical compatibility concerns differing systems or standards; here the systems are already compatible.
Cybersecurity threats concern disruption or manipulation of networks.
Operational environment concerns distance, terrain, mobility and degraded communications.

questions.stem: Signal support enables participating forces to coordinate actions, exchange reports, synchronize activities, and maintain a shared understanding of the operation. Which role of signal support in coalition operations is primarily being described?
questions.explanation: Enhancing coordination is the role of letting forces coordinate actions, exchange reports, synchronize activities and keep a shared understanding of the operation.
why: That role is about protecting mission-critical information.
That role is about managing differences among coalition partners, which the stem does not stress.
That is a key component about sustaining and restoring capability, not a role.

questions.stem: In a coalition operation, two forces may both have functioning radios but still be unable to exchange information because their systems or procedures are not compatible. The Signal Officer must identify the gap before the operation and coordinate a workable solution. Which key component of signal support is being described?
questions.explanation: Interoperability means systems, equipment, procedures and users can work together enough to support the mission. Two forces with working radios that still cannot exchange information have an interoperability gap.
why: Secure communication concerns protecting information, not a compatibility gap.
Scalable systems concerns adjusting to growth in users and locations.
Technical support and maintenance concerns equipment readiness and restoration of service.

questions.stem: What is the main purpose of Signal Support in military operations?
questions.key: To enable communication, coordination and information exchange
distractors: To fire and maneuver against enemy forces directly
To replace the commander's decision-making authority
To collect intelligence on enemy dispositions
questions.explanation: Signal support provides and sustains the communication and information capabilities that let forces communicate, coordinate and exchange information, so commanders can exercise command and control.
why: Engaging the enemy is the task of maneuver and fires units, not signal support.
Signal support supports the commander's decision-making; it does not replace it.
Intelligence collection is an intelligence function, not the main purpose of signal support.

questions.stem: Suspicious activity is detected on a headquarters network. Which response follows the handout?
questions.key: Report through prescribed channels and involve authorized incident responders
distractors: Wait for a user complaint before taking any action
Shut down the network and wipe all devices without informing anyone
Let the local operator resolve it quietly without responders
questions.explanation: Suspicious network activity is reported through established procedures. Designated incident responders (such as CSIRT) investigate and direct the corrective actions.
why: Waiting delays detection and containment of a possible compromise.
Unreported wiping destroys evidence and disrupts operations without coordination.
Without responders the extent of compromise is not properly investigated.

questions.stem: A deployed radio is reported lost during a joint operation. What should the responsible personnel do?
questions.key: Report the possible compromise and implement directed protective actions under prescribed procedures
distractors: Treat it as a routine supply loss and replace it without reporting
Keep using the same frequencies until the radio is found
Wait until the radio is recovered before telling anyone
questions.explanation: Lost communication equipment may fall into adversary hands and compromise operational frequencies. It is treated as a possible security incident: report it through prescribed channels and carry out the directed protective actions.
why: A supply-only response ignores the security risk to the wider network.
Continued use of possibly compromised frequencies exposes operations.
Delaying the report postpones frequency changes and other protection.

questions.stem: An Air Force element joins an existing Army-Navy mission. The signal officer adds required links and capacity while retaining agreed procedures. Which principle is most directly applied?
questions.explanation: Scalability means signal support expands and is tailored as the size, situation and phases of an operation change. Adding links and capacity for a joining Air Force element applies this principle.
why: Operations Focused is about designing support around the mission, not expanding for a new element.
Redundant is about backup paths when a system fails.
Secured is about complying with COMSEC regardless of technology.

questions.stem: A force has ten radios, but three are unserviceable and some remaining sets lack trained operators. What should the planner base the support plan on?
questions.key: Actual usable equipment capability and available trained personnel
distractors: The total number of radios in the inventory
The unit's authorized equipment list on paper
The equipment the unit would ideally like to have
questions.explanation: Planners should count usable capability, not just equipment on hand. Unserviceable sets and untrained operators reduce what the force can really field.
why: The raw inventory includes unserviceable radios and untrained operators.
An authorized list says nothing about what is serviceable and operated.
Wished-for equipment is not available to support the mission.

questions.stem: The joint force shifts from maritime transport to securing land objectives, and the Army becomes the supported component. What should the signal officer do?
questions.key: Update the estimate, links, responsibilities, and priorities for the new phase
distractors: Keep the original estimate and links unchanged
Preserve the earlier maritime support arrangement only
Wait until the phase ends before revising the plan
questions.explanation: Support must be scalable and adapt as the force moves into another phase. When the Army becomes the supported component, the signal officer updates the estimate, links, responsibilities and priorities.
why: An unchanged estimate reflects the maritime phase, not the new land mission.
The earlier arrangement no longer matches the supported component and objectives.
Waiting until the phase ends leaves the force without suitable support during it.

questions.stem: An infantry company and an armored element have functioning radios but cannot exchange required information because their systems and arrangements are incompatible. What should the signal planner address first?
distractors: Buy more radios of the same type for both elements
Increase the transmitter power of the existing radios
Rely permanently on messengers for all reports
questions.explanation: Interoperability means systems are compatible and follow standardized arrangements. Owning radios does not guarantee units can exchange information, so the planner first establishes compatible arrangements.
why: More of the same radios does not fix incompatible arrangements.
Higher power does not make incompatible systems work together.
Permanent messengers abandon radio communication instead of solving the incompatibility.

questions.stem: During the network build-out phase, signal personnel implement a specific monitoring tool that systematically collects and analyzes log activity across various IT resources to detect anomalies. Which specific security and monitoring function is being described?
questions.explanation: SIEM collects and analyzes log activity across IT resources, helping detect anomalies. Security monitoring begins while the network is being built.
why: Cyber risk assessment measures compliance with security controls rather than analyzing logs.
NAC enforces access policies for users and devices.
VAPT identifies weaknesses in the network infrastructure; it does not continuously analyze logs.

questions.stem: Army units and civilian responders need to coordinate relief activities after a disaster. Which communication arrangement follows the handout?
questions.key: Establish a response net separate from the secured Army operational net
distractors: Put civilian responders on the secured Army operational net
Share Army cipher material with all civilian agencies
Prohibit any communication with civilian responders
questions.explanation: In humanitarian assistance and disaster response, the response radio net is kept separate from the Army's secured operational net so civilian coordination does not expose secured traffic.
why: That would expose the secured net to non-Army users.
Handing out cipher material compromises security.
Relief coordination needs communication with responders, so a ban defeats the purpose.

questions.stem: A commander must communicate through a vigilance net after other means fail. How should signal personnel treat the net?
questions.key: Apply authorized protection measures and recognize its continuing interception risk
distractors: Treat it as fully secure once ciphertext and double talk are used
Skip protection measures because the net is authorized
Use it as the primary net for all routine traffic
questions.explanation: The vigilance net operates in a less secure mode and is open to attack and eavesdropping. Ciphertext and double talk mitigate this but do not make the net fully secure.
why: Those measures only mitigate the risk; the net stays vulnerable.
Protection measures are still required on a less secure net.
It is a fallback after other means fail, not a primary net.

questions.stem: Distance, terrain, mobility, dispersed forces, changing command relationships, and degraded communications can affect Signal support. What key factor affecting coalition signal support is being highlighted here?
questions.explanation: Distance, terrain, mobility, dispersed forces, changing command relationships and degraded communications make up the operational environment challenge.
why: Technical compatibility concerns different systems and standards.
Cybersecurity threats concern disruption or manipulation of networks.
Language and cultural barriers concern terminology, procedures and habits.

questions.stem: A tactical radio is lost and may have fallen into adversary hands. What is the appropriate response?
questions.key: Report the incident and follow prescribed compromise and coordinated change procedures
distractors: Search quietly and report only if the adversary is confirmed to have it
Keep operating on the same frequencies pending confirmation
Replace the set and file only a supply report
questions.explanation: A lost radio may expose operational frequencies. It is reported through prescribed channels and the directed procedures, including coordinated changes to affected frequencies, are carried out.
why: Waiting for confirmation of capture delays the protective action.
Continuing on compromised frequencies gives the adversary access.
A supply report alone does not trigger frequency changes.

questions.stem: A coalition command post loses a critical communication capability during an operation. The problem may not be solved simply by 'restarting the radio.' The Signal element must identify the fault, determine whether an alternate means is available, coordinate with the affected user, and restore the required capability as quickly as practical. Which key component of signal support in coalition operations is primarily being tested or addressed through this troubleshooting and restoration process?
questions.explanation: Technical support and maintenance covers troubleshooting, equipment readiness and timely restoration of service. Finding the fault, using an alternate and restoring capability is this component.
why: Interoperability is about systems and procedures working together.
Secure communication is about protecting information.
Scalable systems is about adjusting to growth.

questions.stem: A unit moves behind a mountain and loses its previously reliable connection. What is the most appropriate planning response?
questions.key: Reassess coverage and propagation, then coordinate suitable alternate support
distractors: Increase transmitter power and stay at the same position
Wait for the unit to regain line of sight on its own
Assume the link will recover without changes
questions.explanation: Terrain such as a mountain can block signals, and a location with good coverage at first may become unsuitable. The planner reassesses coverage and propagation and coordinates alternate support.
why: More power does not overcome terrain blockage.
Waiting leaves the unit without communication.
Assuming recovery ignores the physical cause of the loss.

questions.stem: During a coalition operation, a unit may need timely updates from another element to maintain a common operational picture. The value is not simply 'more data'; it is delivering relevant information to the users who need it. Which key component of signal support in coalition operations is being described?
questions.explanation: Real-time data sharing is delivering timely, relevant information to the users who need it, supporting a common operational picture and decisions.
why: Interoperability concerns systems and procedures working together.
Secure communication concerns protecting information.
Technical support and maintenance concerns equipment readiness and restoration.

questions.stem: Commanders need reliable means to issue guidance, receive reports, and make decisions. Signal support therefore directly contributes to command and control. Which role of signal support in coalition operations is primarily being described?
questions.explanation: Facilitating command and control means commanders have reliable means to issue guidance, receive reports and make decisions, so signal support directly contributes to command and control.
why: That role is about protecting mission-critical information.
That role is about managing differences among coalition partners.
That is a key component about equipment readiness and restoration, not a role.

questions.stem: A platoon proposes using a convenient commercial application to send sensitive operational reports. What should be checked before use?
questions.key: Whether its use is authorized and meets applicable COMSEC requirements
distractors: Whether it is popular and easy for the platoon to use
Whether it is free of charge
Whether the platoon leader personally prefers it
questions.explanation: A convenient application must be assessed against COMSEC policy before it carries operational information. Availability does not mean every type of military information may be sent through it.
why: Popularity and ease of use do not make it secure.
Cost has no bearing on security authorization.
Personal preference is not a security criterion.

questions.stem: Signal support must protect mission-critical information and communication capabilities. Security considerations should be built into planning and operation not added only after a problem occurs. Which role of signal support in coalition operations is primarily being described?
questions.explanation: Strengthening operational security means protecting mission-critical information and capabilities, with security built into planning and operation rather than added after a problem.
why: That role is about letting forces coordinate and share understanding.
That role is about giving commanders reliable means to issue guidance and receive reports.
That role is about managing partner differences.

questions.stem: What does Signal Support to Combined Arms Operations enable?
distractors: Replacement of infantry and armor units by signal units
Exclusive use of commercial networks for all reporting
Independent operation of each branch without information exchange
questions.explanation: Signal support to combined arms lets infantry, armor, artillery, engineers and other elements exchange orders, reports and requests so their capabilities work together.
why: Signal units support, not replace, maneuver units.
Commercial networks are not exclusive and must meet COMSEC requirements.
Combined arms depends on information exchange, not independent operation.

questions.stem: In a fast-moving combined arms operation, primary communication lines may be disrupted by terrain or enemy action. Identifying backup radio frequencies, alternate routing, and rapid restoration capabilities addresses which pillar of the Philippine Army Signal Operations Framework?
questions.explanation: Recover covers alternate paths, backup frequencies, alternate routing and rapid restoration when communication is disrupted by terrain or enemy action.
why: Connect establishes connectivity among units.
Sustain maintains connectivity throughout operations.
Secured is a principle about COMSEC, not a pillar of the framework.

questions.stem: Different forces may use different systems or technical standards. A working system is not necessarily an interoperable system. Which major challenge in coalition operations does this statement primarily highlight?
questions.explanation: A working system is not necessarily interoperable: different forces may use different systems or technical standards. This is the technical compatibility challenge.
why: Cybersecurity threats concern disruption or manipulation of networks.
Language and cultural barriers concern terminology and habits.
Operational environment concerns distance, terrain and mobility.

questions.stem: A storm disables the primary link between the joint headquarters and an Army unit. A tested alternate is available. What is the best response?
questions.key: Use the planned alternate and coordinate diagnosis and restoration of the primary link
distractors: Suspend headquarters-unit communication until the primary link returns
Use a commercial application without checking its authorization
Wait for new orders before using the alternate
questions.explanation: A tested alternate keeps communication going while the primary is diagnosed and restored, in line with PACE and redundancy planning.
why: Suspending communication wastes the tested alternate.
An unchecked commercial application may breach COMSEC.
The alternate is already planned and tested; waiting delays communication unnecessarily.

questions.stem: When establishing security controls for a new signal network, signal personnel conduct a review to measure how well the network complies with the security controls referenced by the manual. Which monitoring and assessment function does this represent?
questions.explanation: A cyber risk assessment measures how well the network complies with the referenced security controls.
why: SIEM collects and analyzes log activity across IT resources.
VAPT identifies weaknesses in the network infrastructure.
SOC monitoring detects and helps react to security incidents.

questions.stem: An Army command post will relocate during a joint mission. Which action best maintains communication support?
questions.key: Plan continuity during movement and assess the new site's coverage and logistics
distractors: Keep communicating only from the old site until the move ends
Plan communications only after arriving at the new site
Assume the new site has the same coverage as the old one
questions.explanation: Communication arrangements must keep connecting forces as they move, and good coverage at one location may not hold at the next. Planners ensure continuity and assess the new site's coverage and logistics.
why: The old site cannot support the unit after it relocates.
Planning only after arrival creates a gap during the move.
Coverage and logistics differ by site and must be assessed.

questions.stem: A unit has serviceable radios but too few charged batteries for a three-day mission with naval support. What should the signal planner do?
questions.key: Arrange power resupply or charging support based on mission duration
distractors: Rely on the current charge and request batteries later
Shorten the mission to fit the battery supply
Use the radios only occasionally to save power
questions.explanation: Operations focused support considers mission duration, equipment readiness and power requirements. Serviceable radios are useless without power, so charging or resupply is planned for the mission.
why: Relying on the current charge risks failure mid-mission.
Changing the mission to fit batteries puts communication ahead of the mission.
Limiting use may deny needed communication.

questions.stem: A coalition operation may expand from a small command post into several dispersed locations. Signal planning must anticipate increased users, traffic, locations, coordination requirements, and contingencies. Which key component of signal support in coalition operations is primarily being described?
questions.explanation: Scalable systems adjust as size, location, tempo and mission change. Planning anticipates more users, traffic, locations and contingencies.
why: Interoperability is about systems and procedures working together.
Real-time data sharing is about timely delivery of relevant information.
Secure communication is about protecting information.

exams.title: Exam on Signal Support in Coalition Operations
exams.portalTitle: Exam on Signal Support in Coalition Operation

questions.stem: An existing coalition Signal plan adequately supports two contingents. A third contingent joins the operation, adding new headquarters, users, locations, and information exchanges, while the original capabilities remain serviceable. What is the BEST planning response?
questions.key: Expand the support arrangement to accommodate the increased requirement while preserving interoperability and security
distractors: Retain the existing arrangement unchanged because the original capabilities remain serviceable
Replace the whole arrangement with a new system for all three contingents, ignoring existing interoperability
Support the third contingent separately without coordinating with the existing arrangement or its security
questions.explanation: Signal support must be scalable: when users, headquarters, locations and exchanges grow, the arrangement is expanded to meet them while keeping interoperability and security intact.
why: The new contingent adds requirements the existing arrangement was not sized for, so leaving it unchanged leaves a gap.
Replacing everything discards working, interoperable capability and adds needless risk.
A separate, uncoordinated arrangement breaks interoperability and weakens security.

questions.stem: During coalition planning, all participating forces can exchange required voice communications. However, one contingent cannot receive a mission-essential digital operational report in a usable form. Which assessment BEST identifies the remaining problem?
questions.key: Information interoperability remains deficient because required information cannot be effectively exchanged and understood
distractors: Technical interoperability is complete because all forces can already exchange voice
Security accreditation is the only remaining problem
No problem remains, since every force can communicate
questions.explanation: Working voice links do not mean the coalition can exchange all required information. The contingent that cannot use the digital report shows a gap in information interoperability.
why: Voice working shows only part of the technical picture; the unusable digital report is still a deficiency.
The stem describes a usability and exchange failure, not a protection failure.
A mission-essential report cannot be used by one contingent, so a problem clearly remains.

questions.stem: During mission analysis, the Signal Officer identifies several available communications systems. One provides excellent connectivity but cannot satisfy the coalition's information-protection requirements. Another is more limited but meets the required information exchange and security conditions. What is the BEST basis for recommending a capability?
questions.key: The capability that best satisfies the total mission requirement, including required information exchange and protection
distractors: The capability with the best connectivity, regardless of protection needs
The newest and most advanced equipment available
The capability most familiar to the lead nation's operators
questions.explanation: The recommendation rests on which capability best meets the total mission requirement, including information exchange and protection. Excellent connectivity does not make up for failing the security requirement.
why: Connectivity alone ignores the stated information-protection requirement.
Equipment novelty is not a mission requirement and does not guarantee the needed protection.
Familiarity to one nation does not show the capability meets the coalition's requirements.

questions.stem: Two coalition contingents successfully establish a technical connection. During operations, however, reports are repeatedly misunderstood because each force uses different procedures and terminology. Which assessment is MOST appropriate?
questions.key: Technical connectivity exists, but procedural and information interoperability remain deficient
distractors: Interoperability is achieved because the technical connection works
Only replacing equipment is needed to stop the misunderstandings
The problem is limited to cybersecurity threats
questions.explanation: A working link is not enough. Different procedures and terminology cause misunderstanding, so procedural and information interoperability must also be addressed.
why: A working connection does not guarantee mutual understanding.
The cause is procedures and terminology, which new equipment does not fix.
The stem describes misunderstandings, not an attack or intrusion.

questions.stem: During planning, the primary communications arrangement satisfies current command and control requirements. Intelligence indicates that the primary means may become unavailable during a critical phase. What is the MOST appropriate Signal planning response?
questions.key: Establish alternative arrangements and actions synchronized with the operational plan before execution
distractors: Accept the risk and rely on the primary means because it meets current requirements
Plan alternates only after the primary means actually fails
Add more users to the primary means to raise its capacity
questions.explanation: Signal support must sustain communications when conditions change. Alternate arrangements and actions should be planned and synchronized with the operational plan before execution.
why: Intelligence indicates a likely loss, so ignoring it leaves the critical phase unprotected.
Planning after failure is too late to sustain command and control in the critical phase.
More users on the same means adds dependence and does not give a fallback.

questions.stem: A participating force requests access to a coalition information service because its system is technically capable of connecting to it. What should PRINCIPALLY determine whether access is authorized?
questions.key: Whether the information is required for the mission and applicable security requirements permit access
distractors: Whether the force's system is technically capable of connecting to the service
Whether the force is a coalition member, regardless of need
Whether the force is the largest contingent in the coalition
questions.explanation: Access depends on mission need and on applicable security requirements. Technical ability to connect does not by itself authorize access.
why: Technical capability is not authorization; it can exist without need or clearance.
Membership alone does not grant access; need and security requirements still apply.
Contingent size is not a criterion for access to information.

questions.stem: During execution, the coalition shifts its main effort, requiring headquarters relocation and changing priority information exchanges. Existing communications remain operational but no longer fully support the revised command and information requirements. What should the Signal Officer do FIRST?
questions.key: Reassess the changed operational requirements and adjust Signal support to the new users, locations, and information exchanges
distractors: Continue with existing communications until a failure is reported
Procure more equipment for the relocated headquarters right away
Wait for the commander to name the equipment to change
questions.explanation: When the main effort and priorities change, the Signal Officer first reassesses the new operational requirements and then adjusts support to the new users, locations and exchanges.
why: Waiting for a failure ignores that current support no longer meets the revised requirements.
Buying equipment before knowing what is required is premature.
The Signal Officer translates requirements into capability; waiting for equipment direction does not do this.

questions.stem: A coalition communications plan identifies required users, systems, and information exchanges, but responsibilities between participating Signal elements remain unclear. Which deficiency presents the MOST immediate planning concern?
questions.key: Support relationships and coordination mechanisms have not been clearly established
distractors: The plan does not specify which brand of equipment each element will use
The plan lists too many users and information exchanges
No common national language has been chosen for all voice traffic
questions.explanation: With requirements identified but responsibilities unclear, the most immediate concern is that support relationships and coordination mechanisms are not established, which leaves nobody accountable for delivering the support.
why: Equipment brand is a secondary detail and does not address unclear responsibilities.
Listing the required users and exchanges is the point of the plan; it is not a deficiency.
Language is a challenge, but the stem's gap is about responsibilities.

questions.stem: Which condition provides the STRONGEST basis for the Signal Officer to assess coalition communications support as ready for execution?
questions.key: Mission-required users and information exchanges are supported, interoperability gaps addressed, responsibilities coordinated, contingencies established, and applicable protection requirements incorporated
distractors: All planned equipment is installed and each system has passed a technical test
Connectivity exists among all headquarters and the commander has approved the plan
The plan mirrors the previous operation's communications and was rehearsed once
questions.explanation: Readiness means required users and exchanges are supported, interoperability gaps are addressed, responsibilities are coordinated, contingencies exist and protection requirements are in place.
why: Installed, tested equipment can still leave gaps in interoperability, coordination, continuity and protection.
Connectivity and approval do not show that interoperability, continuity and security are covered.
Copying a past operation does not show this mission's requirements are met.

questions.stem: A coalition headquarters directs the Signal planning team to immediately identify radios and network equipment for an upcoming operation. Mission analysis and user requirements have not yet been completed. What is the BEST response by the Signal Officer?
questions.key: Determine the mission, command, information, and user requirements before matching available capabilities against them
distractors: Issue the available radios and network equipment now and adapt requirements later
Select the most capable equipment in stock first and ask for user needs afterward
Wait for partner nations to submit equipment lists before analyzing requirements
questions.explanation: Requirements come first: the Signal Officer determines mission, command, information and user needs, then matches capabilities against them. Choosing equipment first risks fitting the mission to the kit.
why: Issuing equipment first reverses the order and risks mismatch with the mission.
Choosing by capability before requirements ignores what the mission needs.
Partner lists do not replace the Signal Officer's own requirements analysis.

questions.stem: During preparation for execution, the Signal Officer discovers that all current communications requirements are supported, but no arrangements exist if the primary means is disrupted. Which conclusion is MOST defensible?
questions.key: The support plan remains incomplete because continuity requirements have not been adequately addressed
distractors: The plan is complete because all current requirements are supported
The plan is complete because continuity is the users' responsibility
The plan is incomplete only because interoperability has not been achieved
questions.explanation: Signal support includes sustaining the capability. With no arrangements if the primary means is disrupted, continuity is unaddressed and the plan remains incomplete.
why: Supporting current requirements alone does not cover the loss of the primary means.
Continuity is a planning responsibility of the Signal Officer, not left to users.
The stem says requirements are supported; the stated gap is continuity, not interoperability.

questions.stem: During coalition mission planning, one contingent reports that its internal communications are fully operational. However, it cannot exchange required operational information with another participating force. What should the Signal Officer assess FIRST?
questions.key: Whether mission-required information exchange and interoperability interfaces have been established
distractors: Whether the contingent's internal systems should be replaced
Whether the contingent needs additional internal communications capacity
Whether the other force should adopt the contingent's national procedures
questions.explanation: A working internal system is not an interoperable one. The first check is whether mission-required information exchange and the interoperability interfaces between the forces have been established.
why: Internal communications already work, so replacing them does not address the exchange problem.
Capacity inside the contingent is not the problem; the issue is exchange with another force.
Forcing one nation's procedures on another is not the first assessment; the interface must be examined first.

questions.stem: A coalition headquarters is preparing to support geographically separated forces. Several communications systems are available, but their suitability has not yet been determined. Which action BEST reflects the proper planning approach?
questions.key: Determine mission, user, information, terrain, security, and continuity requirements before selecting capabilities
distractors: Select the most capable available systems first, then confirm requirements
Choose the systems the lead nation already uses and apply them to all forces
Issue the same standard communications package to every force
questions.explanation: Suitability is judged against requirements, so the Signal Officer first determines mission, user, information, terrain, security and continuity needs and then selects capabilities.
why: Selecting systems before requirements reverses the correct order.
Using the lead nation's systems by default ignores the stated requirements and the need for interoperability.
An identical package ignores differences in location, users and needs among separated forces.

exams.title: Exam on Signal Support in Joint Operations
exams.portalTitle: Exam on Signal Support in Joint Operation

questions.stem: The joint force shifts from maritime transport to securing land objectives, and the Army becomes the supported component. What should the signal officer do?
questions.key: Update the estimate, links, responsibilities, and priorities for the new phase
distractors: Keep the original estimate and links unchanged
Preserve the earlier maritime support arrangement only
Wait until the phase ends before revising the plan
questions.explanation: Support must be scalable and adapt as the force moves into another phase. When the Army becomes the supported component, the signal officer updates the estimate, links, responsibilities and priorities.
why: An unchanged estimate reflects the maritime phase, not the new land mission.
The earlier arrangement no longer matches the supported component and objectives.
Waiting until the phase ends leaves the force without suitable support during it.

questions.stem: Which principle applies when the network expands to include an additional service component?
questions.explanation: Scalable means signal support can adapt when forces or requirements change, such as when another service component joins the network.
why: Redundancy provides backup paths in case a link fails; it is not about growing the network.
Secured concerns protecting communications, not accommodating added components.
Operations Focused means support serves the commander's mission; it is not the principle about expansion.

questions.stem: A plan provides a tested alternative path if the main link fails. Which principle does this demonstrate?
questions.explanation: Redundancy means essential communication can continue through multiple paths or backup means when a link fails, which a tested alternate path provides.
why: Scalable is about adapting to changes in force size, not about backup paths.
Interoperable is about compatibility between systems and services, not alternate paths.
Secured is about protecting communications, not providing a fallback link.

questions.stem: What is the main contribution of signal support to joint command and control?
questions.key: It enables timely exchange of decisions and reports across participating forces
distractors: It replaces the need for a single commander over the joint force
It decides the operational objectives of each participating service
It controls the physical movement of maneuver units
questions.explanation: Signal support connects the participating services so commanders can communicate decisions and coordinate the forces assigned to the operation, supporting command and control.
why: Joint operations still work under a single commander; signal support does not replace that command.
Objectives come from the commander and operational planning, not from signal support.
Signal support carries information for command and control; it does not direct unit movement.

questions.stem: A joint headquarters needs IP-based telephone calls over its authorized data network. Which technology best meets this requirement?
questions.explanation: VoIP carries telephone calls over IP data networks, so it fits a headquarters that needs IP-based telephony over its authorized data network.
why: NAC only enforces policies on which users and devices may access the network; it does not carry calls.
A UTM firewall filters traffic and detects intrusions; it is not a telephony technology.
SIEM collects and analyzes log activity for security monitoring; it does not carry voice calls.

questions.stem: A unit has serviceable radios but too few charged batteries for a three-day mission with naval support. What should the signal planner do?
questions.key: Arrange power resupply or charging support based on mission duration
distractors: Rely on the current charge and request batteries later
Shorten the mission to fit the battery supply
Use the radios only occasionally to save power
questions.explanation: Operations focused support considers mission duration, equipment readiness and power requirements. Serviceable radios are useless without power, so charging or resupply is planned for the mission.
why: Relying on the current charge risks failure mid-mission.
Changing the mission to fit batteries puts communication ahead of the mission.
Limiting use may deny needed communication.

questions.stem: Which security technology enforces access policies for users and devices?
questions.explanation: Network Access Control (NAC) enforces policies governing access by users and devices.
why: Endpoint security protects individual computers with antivirus and device controls, not access policy for users and devices.
Unified Threat Management combines filtering, anti-malware and intrusion detection rather than enforcing access policy.
Frequency hopping is an electronic protection measure against jamming and interception, not an access control technology.

questions.stem: An Air Force element joins an existing Army-Navy mission. The signal officer adds required links and capacity while retaining agreed procedures. Which principle is most directly applied?
questions.explanation: Scalability means signal support expands and is tailored as the size, situation and phases of an operation change. Adding links and capacity for a joining Air Force element applies this principle.
why: Operations Focused is about designing support around the mission, not expanding for a new element.
Redundant is about backup paths when a system fails.
Secured is about complying with COMSEC regardless of technology.

questions.stem: What should the signal planner determine before selecting communication equipment?
questions.key: The mission, communication requirements, and factors affecting support
distractors: Only the number of radios already issued to the unit
The equipment brand preferred by the signal officer
Only the cost and delivery schedule of new equipment
questions.explanation: Before choosing equipment the planner must understand the mission, who needs to communicate with whom, and the factors that affect support such as terrain, resources and threats.
why: Equipment on hand is one resource to check, but selection starts from the mission and requirements, not from inventory alone.
Preference for a brand does not reflect mission or requirements.
Cost and delivery alone ignore what the mission needs and the conditions of support.

questions.stem: What is the proper basis for using a commercial communication platform for military information?
questions.key: Authorization under applicable COMSEC policies and information requirements
distractors: The platform is available and convenient to use
The platform is widely used by partner services
The speed of the platform compared with military systems
questions.explanation: Commercial platforms may be used only under applicable COMSEC policies and with regard to what information they may carry; being available does not mean any military information may be sent through them.
why: Availability alone does not make a device suitable for every type of military information.
Popularity with partners does not authorize use under COMSEC policy.
Speed does not determine authorization or protection of information.

questions.stem: Which system provides a secured and managed Army intranet?
questions.explanation: PANET is the Philippine Army Network, which provides a secured, managed Army intranet.
why: Radio over IP links radio communications through IP networks; it is not the Army intranet.
Combat Net Radio provides radio networks for operating units, not an intranet.
BONTEX is a telephone exchange, not the managed Army intranet.

questions.stem: How should communication resources be allocated when requirements exceed available capability?
questions.key: Prioritize requirements according to mission importance and commander's guidance
distractors: Divide capacity equally among all requesters
Serve requests in the order they were submitted
Reduce every requirement until it fits regardless of importance
questions.explanation: When requirements exceed capability, support is prioritized according to mission importance and the commander's guidance, for example essential command links first.
why: Equal sharing can leave essential command links short of capacity.
First-come order ignores mission importance and the commander's priorities.
Cutting all requirements blindly ignores which ones the mission depends on.

questions.stem: A commander must communicate through a vigilance net after other means fail. How should signal personnel treat the net?
questions.key: Apply authorized protection measures and recognize its continuing interception risk
distractors: Treat it as fully secure once ciphertext and double talk are used
Skip protection measures because the net is authorized
Use it as the primary net for all routine traffic
questions.explanation: The vigilance net operates in a less secure mode and is open to attack and eavesdropping. Ciphertext and double talk mitigate this but do not make the net fully secure.
why: Those measures only mitigate the risk; the net stays vulnerable.
Protection measures are still required on a less secure net.
It is a fallback after other means fail, not a primary net.

questions.stem: Which capability allows a commander to establish an operations center away from a fixed facility?
questions.explanation: A Mobile Command Center lets the commander set up an operations center wherever he chooses, equipped with the C4S capabilities needed to lead.
why: A fixed operations center is tied to a facility, which is what the stem moves away from.
Tactical communication is military-grade communication for troops on the move and on the halt, not a command facility.
Special purpose communication refers to commercial devices that augment routine communication, not a mobile command facility.

questions.stem: Which statement best guides selection of tactical radios for a joint force?
questions.key: Compatibility, configuration, and agreed procedures must be verified
distractors: Choose the newest radio model regardless of other services' equipment
Each service uses its own radios and procedures without coordination
Prefer the radios with the highest transmit power
questions.explanation: Radios from different services must be checked for compatibility, configuration and agreed procedures so they can actually work together.
why: The newest model may not be compatible with other services' radios.
Uncoordinated use defeats interoperability in a joint force.
Power does not ensure compatibility, configuration or common procedures.

questions.stem: An Army command post will relocate during a joint mission. Which action best maintains communication support?
questions.key: Plan continuity during movement and assess the new site's coverage and logistics
distractors: Keep communicating only from the old site until the move ends
Plan communications only after arriving at the new site
Assume the new site has the same coverage as the old one
questions.explanation: Communication arrangements must keep connecting forces as they move, and good coverage at one location may not hold at the next. Planners ensure continuity and assess the new site's coverage and logistics.
why: The old site cannot support the unit after it relocates.
Planning only after arrival creates a gap during the move.
Coverage and logistics differ by site and must be assessed.

questions.stem: Why embed an Air Force radio operator at an Army tactical operations center?
questions.key: To facilitate direct coordination with supporting air assets
distractors: To replace the Army radio operators at subordinate units
To provide cyber protection for the operations center network
To issue the CEOI to all participating services
questions.explanation: An Air Force radio operator at an Army tactical operations center helps the commander communicate with and coordinate the supporting air assets directly.
why: The embedded operator relays coordination with air assets; he does not replace Army operators.
Network cyber protection is a separate function, not the purpose of the embedded operator.
CEOI issuance is not the role of an embedded radio operator.

questions.stem: Which assessment best determines whether radios can support a prolonged deployment?
questions.key: Check serviceability, trained operators, power, and maintenance support
distractors: Count the radios issued regardless of their condition
Confirm that the radios are the latest commercial model
Compare radio prices from different suppliers
questions.explanation: Sustaining a prolonged deployment depends on whether radios are serviceable, operators are trained, power is available and maintenance support exists.
why: A count says nothing about serviceability or the ability to keep radios working.
Being the newest model does not show they can be sustained.
Price comparison does not assess whether radios can be supported over time.

questions.stem: Which set correctly describes PACE communication arrangements?
questions.explanation: PACE stands for Primary, Alternate, Contingency, and Emergency, the order of communication means used when others fail.
why: The second means is Alternate, not Authorized.
The third means is Contingency, not Control.
PACE begins with Primary and ends with Emergency; the other terms are not part of it.

questions.stem: A storm disables the primary link between the joint headquarters and an Army unit. A tested alternate is available. What is the best response?
questions.key: Use the planned alternate and coordinate diagnosis and restoration of the primary link
distractors: Suspend headquarters-unit communication until the primary link returns
Use a commercial application without checking its authorization
Wait for new orders before using the alternate
questions.explanation: A tested alternate keeps communication going while the primary is diagnosed and restored, in line with PACE and redundancy planning.
why: Suspending communication wastes the tested alternate.
An unchecked commercial application may breach COMSEC.
The alternate is already planned and tested; waiting delays communication unnecessarily.

questions.stem: A joint network operator detects suspicious activity affecting Army and Navy systems. What is the most appropriate action?
questions.key: Report through established channels and activate coordinated incident-response procedures
distractors: Disconnect all Army and Navy systems permanently and delete the logs
Investigate and repair it alone without informing anyone
Ignore the activity until it affects mission traffic
questions.explanation: Suspicious activity is reported through established procedures, and designated incident responders investigate and direct corrective action. In joint operations the Army and Navy responses are coordinated.
why: Permanent disconnection and deleting logs destroys evidence and the joint capability.
Acting alone bypasses the responders who investigate the extent of compromise.
Waiting allows a possible compromise to spread unreported.

questions.stem: Which arrangement best illustrates a joint operation?
questions.key: Army and Navy forces executing a common mission under one commander
distractors: Infantry, armor, artillery and engineers working together under an Army commander
Two Army brigades pursuing a common mission under one division
Army and Navy forces pursuing separate missions under separate commanders
questions.explanation: A joint operation involves two or more AFP services, such as the Army and Navy, working under a single commander to accomplish a common mission.
why: That is a combined arms operation within one service, not a joint one.
Both units belong to one service, so it is not a joint operation.
Joint operations share a common mission under a single commander.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly distinguishes CEOI from CESI?
questions.key: CEOI provides operating instructions; CESI explains how to use the CEOI items
distractors: CESI provides the operating instructions; CEOI explains how to use the CESI items
CEOI and CESI are the same document under different names
CEOI covers cyber protection while CESI covers equipment repair
questions.explanation: CEOI provides the operating instructions, while CESI explains how to use the items in the CEOI.
why: This reverses the roles; the CEOI holds the instructions and the CESI explains their use.
They are distinct documents with different purposes.
Neither document is about cyber protection or equipment repair.

questions.stem: Which technology links radio communication through an IP network?
questions.explanation: Radio over IP (ROIP) links radio communication through an IP network.
why: Network Access Control enforces access policy; it does not carry radio traffic.
A Mobile Command Center is a command facility, not a radio-linking technology.
Frequency hopping is an electronic protection technique, not a link to an IP network.

questions.stem: Which action best validates a tentative joint signal plan?
questions.key: Verify links, coverage gaps, resources, responsibilities, and security with the services
distractors: Issue the plan right away without coordination with the services
Confirm only that enough radios were issued
Wait to test the plan during the actual operation
questions.explanation: A tentative plan is validated by verifying links, coverage gaps, resources, responsibilities and security with the services involved.
why: Skipping coordination leaves gaps and conflicts unchecked.
Radio count alone does not verify links, coverage, responsibilities or security.
Validation should happen before the operation, not during it.

questions.stem: An Army unit ashore receives delayed messages from a supporting naval element because their systems cannot communicate directly. What is the best signal support action?
questions.key: Coordinate compatible equipment or an approved embedded-operator relay arrangement
distractors: Wait for the naval element to replace its systems with Army equipment
Send the traffic over unprotected commercial applications
Stop exchanging messages until the operation ends
questions.explanation: Joint signal support bridges gaps between services through compatible equipment and coordinated radio operators. An Army operator embedded with the naval element can relay information between troops ashore and the naval support.
why: Waiting for a wholesale equipment replacement is impractical and leaves the delay unresolved.
Unprotected commercial applications do not satisfy COMSEC requirements for operational traffic.
Stopping the exchange removes the coordination the joint force needs.

questions.stem: A deployed radio is reported lost during a joint operation. What should the responsible personnel do?
questions.key: Report the possible compromise and implement directed protective actions under prescribed procedures
distractors: Treat it as a routine supply loss and replace it without reporting
Keep using the same frequencies until the radio is found
Wait until the radio is recovered before telling anyone
questions.explanation: Lost communication equipment may fall into adversary hands and compromise operational frequencies. It is treated as a possible security incident: report it through prescribed channels and carry out the directed protective actions.
why: A supply-only response ignores the security risk to the wider network.
Continued use of possibly compromised frequencies exposes operations.
Delaying the report postpones frequency changes and other protection.

questions.stem: Why coordinate electromagnetic spectrum use among participating units?
questions.key: To manage frequency requirements and reduce interference
distractors: To select the encryption keys of each unit
To assign operators to each service
To raise the transmit power of all radios
questions.explanation: Units use different technologies and frequencies, so spectrum use is coordinated to manage frequency requirements and reduce interference.
why: Encryption keys are COMSEC matters, not the purpose of spectrum coordination.
Operator assignment is a personnel matter, not spectrum use.
Higher power would increase interference rather than reduce it.

questions.stem: Which planning decision best demonstrates the operations focused principle?
questions.key: Match communication support to the commander's mission requirements
distractors: Select the most advanced technology available
Standardize all services on one equipment brand
Restrict communication to the minimum to reduce cost
questions.explanation: Operations Focused means communication support is matched to the commander's mission requirements.
why: Advanced technology is not the test; the mission requirement is.
Standardizing equipment is not what this principle asks, and it may not serve the mission.
Cost-driven restriction can limit mission execution, which this principle avoids.

questions.stem: Which factor should be assessed when a proposed link crosses a mountain range?
distractors: Rank of the operators at each end
questions.explanation: Mountains affect line-of-sight communication, so terrain effects must be assessed when a link crosses a mountain range.
why: Platform availability does not address the terrain obstruction.
Billing has nothing to do with whether the signal path is blocked.
Operator rank does not affect radio line of sight.

exams.title: Exam on Signal Support in Combined Arms Operations
exams.portalTitle: Exam on Signal Support in Combined Arms Operation

questions.stem: The primary communication link fails during an operation, but an authorized alternate arrangement was established beforehand. What should personnel do?
questions.key: Use the planned alternate arrangement while restoration is coordinated
distractors: Halt all reporting until the primary link is repaired
Switch to any available commercial application without checking authorization
Wait for orders to create an alternate arrangement after the failure
questions.explanation: Redundancy and PACE planning prepare recovery arrangements before disruption. When the primary link fails, personnel already know the authorized alternate, use it to keep communicating, and coordinate repair of the primary.
why: Stopping communication defeats the purpose of a pre-established alternate.
An unauthorized commercial application may not meet COMSEC requirements.
The alternate was already established beforehand; waiting to create one wastes the preparation.

questions.stem: What does Sustain mean in the Connect, Sustain, and Recover framework?
distractors: Repair and restore communication when it is attacked or destroyed
questions.explanation: In Connect, Sustain, and Recover, Sustain means maintaining connectivity throughout operations.
why: That is Connect, the first step.
That is Recover, the third step.
That describes confidentiality, a security concern, not a framework step.

questions.stem: What does Operations Focused require?
questions.key: Communication support must serve the mission and avoid limiting its execution
distractors: Communication networks must use the newest technology available
The mission must be adjusted to fit the available communication system
All units must use identical equipment
questions.explanation: Operations Focused means signal support is built to serve the mission and must not restrict how it is carried out.
why: Technology is a means, not the requirement of this principle.
This reverses the principle; support serves the mission, not the other way round.
Identical equipment relates to standardization, not to being operations focused.

questions.stem: Which principle provides multiple transmission paths and backup capabilities?
questions.explanation: Redundant provides multiple transmission paths and backup capabilities so communication continues if one path fails.
why: Scalable is about adapting to changes in force size and phase.
Interoperable is about compatibility and standardization between systems.
Secured is about protecting communications.

questions.stem: A typhoon damages headquarters communication facilities. Which action most directly applies the Recover function?
questions.key: Deploy appropriate teams to repair and restore communication
distractors: Establish first-time connectivity among Army units that have no links yet
Maintain connectivity through routine inspection and refresher training
Apply network access control policies to all users and devices
questions.explanation: Recover means bringing communication back when facilities, equipment or networks are damaged by a disaster or attack. Signal teams deploy to repair or restore the connections so commanders can resume directing their units.
why: That is the Connect function, which establishes links rather than repairing damaged ones.
That is the Sustain function (maintenance), which keeps working equipment serviceable rather than restoring damaged facilities.
That is an access-control security measure and does not restore a typhoon-damaged facility.

questions.stem: Which characteristic refers to cooperation with agencies, organizations, and partner nations?
questions.explanation: Collective Environment refers to operations involving cooperation with government agencies, nongovernment organizations and partner nations.
why: Disaster-Prone concerns natural calamities and disaster response.
Highly Urbanized concerns buildings, obstacles and civilians.
Archipelagic concerns islands, mountains and bodies of water.

questions.stem: Which principle requires Signal Support to adapt to changing force size and phases of operations?
questions.explanation: Scalable means signal support adapts to changes in force size and to the phases of an operation.
why: Redundant means backup paths, not adapting to force size.
Interoperable means compatibility between systems.
Secured means protection of communications.

questions.stem: What does Signal Support to Combined Arms Operations enable?
distractors: Replacement of infantry and armor units by signal units
Exclusive use of commercial networks for all reporting
Independent operation of each branch without information exchange
questions.explanation: Signal support to combined arms lets infantry, armor, artillery, engineers and other elements exchange orders, reports and requests so their capabilities work together.
why: Signal units support, not replace, maneuver units.
Commercial networks are not exclusive and must meet COMSEC requirements.
Combined arms depends on information exchange, not independent operation.

questions.stem: Which document explains how to use the items in the CEOI?
questions.explanation: CESI, the Communication-Electronics Standing Instructions, explains how to use the items in the CEOI.
why: The CEOI is the document being explained, not the one that explains it.
A signal estimate is a planning analysis, not instructions on using CEOI items.
The signal plan publishes arrangements; it does not explain CEOI items.

questions.stem: A force has ten radios, but three are unserviceable and some remaining sets lack trained operators. What should the planner base the support plan on?
questions.key: Actual usable equipment capability and available trained personnel
distractors: The total number of radios in the inventory
The unit's authorized equipment list on paper
The equipment the unit would ideally like to have
questions.explanation: Planners should count usable capability, not just equipment on hand. Unserviceable sets and untrained operators reduce what the force can really field.
why: The raw inventory includes unserviceable radios and untrained operators.
An authorized list says nothing about what is serviceable and operated.
Wished-for equipment is not available to support the mission.

questions.stem: Which list contains the three Signal Operations environments?
questions.explanation: The three signal operations environments are physical, cyberspace and electromagnetic spectrum.
why: Those are operating domains of services, not signal operations environments.
Those are the three domains inside cyberspace, not the three environments.
Those are communication service types, not environments.

questions.stem: An infantry company and an armored element have functioning radios but cannot exchange required information because their systems and arrangements are incompatible. What should the signal planner address first?
distractors: Buy more radios of the same type for both elements
Increase the transmitter power of the existing radios
Rely permanently on messengers for all reports
questions.explanation: Interoperability means systems are compatible and follow standardized arrangements. Owning radios does not guarantee units can exchange information, so the planner first establishes compatible arrangements.
why: More of the same radios does not fix incompatible arrangements.
Higher power does not make incompatible systems work together.
Permanent messengers abandon radio communication instead of solving the incompatibility.

questions.stem: A tactical radio is lost and may have fallen into adversary hands. What is the appropriate response?
questions.key: Report the incident and follow prescribed compromise and coordinated change procedures
distractors: Search quietly and report only if the adversary is confirmed to have it
Keep operating on the same frequencies pending confirmation
Replace the set and file only a supply report
questions.explanation: A lost radio may expose operational frequencies. It is reported through prescribed channels and the directed procedures, including coordinated changes to affected frequencies, are carried out.
why: Waiting for confirmation of capture delays the protective action.
Continuing on compromised frequencies gives the adversary access.
A supply report alone does not trigger frequency changes.

questions.stem: An engineer element joins the force after the signal plan has been prepared. What should the planner do?
questions.key: Confirm its requirements and compatibility, then update and coordinate the plan
distractors: Keep the existing signal plan unchanged because it was already approved
Tell the engineers to use whatever equipment they brought, without coordination
Cancel the plan and wait for a completely new one from higher headquarters
questions.explanation: Signal support must be scalable: it expands and is tailored when units join. The planner confirms the newcomer's communication needs and compatibility, then updates and coordinates the plan to accommodate the added users.
why: An unchanged plan does not cover the added users and coordination requirements.
Uncoordinated equipment may be incompatible and leave the engineers unable to communicate with the force.
The plan only needs to be adjusted for the new element; discarding it and waiting leaves the force without support.

questions.stem: What does the letter L represent in METAL?
questions.explanation: In METAL (Mission, Enemy, Troops, Area of Operations, Logistical Requirements), L stands for Logistical Requirements.
why: Area of Operations is the fourth letter, A.
Troops is the third letter, T.
METAL has no line-of-sight item; L is Logistical Requirements.

questions.stem: What is PANET according to the handout?
distractors: A radio network for troops on the move
A firewall configuration in the logical domain
A telephone exchange serving fixed headquarters
questions.explanation: PANET, the Philippine Army Network, provides a secured, managed Army intranet.
why: Radio networks are CNR and tactical radio systems, not PANET.
Firewall configuration is part of the logical domain, not what PANET is.
Telephone exchanges are separate from PANET.

questions.stem: What does Radio over IP do?
questions.key: Links radio communications through IP networks
distractors: Enforces access policies for users and devices
Provides a secured, managed Army intranet
Establishes an operations center away from fixed facilities
questions.explanation: Radio over IP (ROIP) links radio communications through IP networks.
why: That is Network Access Control.
That is PANET.
That is the Mobile Command Center.

questions.stem: Army units and civilian responders need to coordinate relief activities after a disaster. Which communication arrangement follows the handout?
questions.key: Establish a response net separate from the secured Army operational net
distractors: Put civilian responders on the secured Army operational net
Share Army cipher material with all civilian agencies
Prohibit any communication with civilian responders
questions.explanation: In humanitarian assistance and disaster response, the response radio net is kept separate from the Army's secured operational net so civilian coordination does not expose secured traffic.
why: That would expose the secured net to non-Army users.
Handing out cipher material compromises security.
Relief coordination needs communication with responders, so a ban defeats the purpose.

questions.stem: How should limited signal resources be prioritized?
questions.key: By supportability and importance to mission accomplishment
distractors: By equipment age and the order in which requests arrive
By the rank of the requesting unit's commander
Equally among all units regardless of their mission
questions.explanation: When requirements exceed capability, planners compare requirements with resources and set priorities by supportability and importance to mission accomplishment, consistent with the commander's guidance and intent.
why: Equipment age and arrival order are not mission-based criteria.
Rank does not determine mission importance or supportability.
Equal sharing ignores mission importance and may starve critical requirements.

questions.stem: Which security concern protects information from unauthorized alteration?
questions.explanation: Integrity means information remains accurate and is not altered without authorization.
why: Confidentiality limits disclosure, not alteration.
Availability keeps the service usable.
Redundancy is a signal support principle, not an information security concern.

questions.stem: A platoon proposes using a convenient commercial application to send sensitive operational reports. What should be checked before use?
questions.key: Whether its use is authorized and meets applicable COMSEC requirements
distractors: Whether it is popular and easy for the platoon to use
Whether it is free of charge
Whether the platoon leader personally prefers it
questions.explanation: A convenient application must be assessed against COMSEC policy before it carries operational information. Availability does not mean every type of military information may be sent through it.
why: Popularity and ease of use do not make it secure.
Cost has no bearing on security authorization.
Personal preference is not a security criterion.

questions.stem: What is the main purpose of Signal Support in military operations?
questions.key: To enable communication, coordination, and information exchange
distractors: To collect and analyze intelligence on enemy forces
To direct the maneuver of combined arms teams
To supply and maintain combat equipment
questions.explanation: Signal support enables communication, coordination and information exchange so commanders and units can accomplish the mission.
why: Intelligence collection is the ISR function.
Direction of maneuver belongs to command and operations.
Supply and maintenance is logistics.

questions.stem: Where are approved signal arrangements formally published?
questions.key: In the Signal Plan or C4S Annex to the operations order or plan
distractors: In the Signal Estimate prepared by the S6
In the CESI issued to each operator
questions.explanation: Approved signal arrangements are put in the Signal Plan or the C4S Annex to the order or plan.
why: The estimate supports planning; it does not publish approved arrangements.
The CESI explains how to use CEOI items.
An after-operations report records results after the event.

questions.stem: Which principle requires compatibility and standardization so units can communicate?
questions.explanation: Interoperable means systems are compatible and standardized so units can communicate with one another.
why: Redundant is about backup paths.
Scalable is about adapting to changes in force size.
Secured is about protecting communications.

questions.stem: Suspicious activity is detected on a headquarters network. Which response follows the handout?
questions.key: Report through prescribed channels and involve authorized incident responders
distractors: Wait for a user complaint before taking any action
Shut down the network and wipe all devices without informing anyone
Let the local operator resolve it quietly without responders
questions.explanation: Suspicious network activity is reported through established procedures. Designated incident responders (such as CSIRT) investigate and direct the corrective actions.
why: Waiting delays detection and containment of a possible compromise.
Unreported wiping destroys evidence and disrupts operations without coordination.
Without responders the extent of compromise is not properly investigated.

questions.stem: A unit moves behind a mountain and loses its previously reliable connection. What is the most appropriate planning response?
questions.key: Reassess coverage and propagation, then coordinate suitable alternate support
distractors: Increase transmitter power and stay at the same position
Wait for the unit to regain line of sight on its own
Assume the link will recover without changes
questions.explanation: Terrain such as a mountain can block signals, and a location with good coverage at first may become unsuitable. The planner reassesses coverage and propagation and coordinates alternate support.
why: More power does not overcome terrain blockage.
Waiting leaves the unit without communication.
Assuming recovery ignores the physical cause of the loss.

questions.stem: Which set correctly identifies the four main Signal Support service categories?
questions.key: Command and control communication; cyberspace operations and electronic warfare; repair and maintenance; recovery and restoration
distractors: Fixed, tactical, special purpose, and operations-center communication
Command and control communication; intelligence and reconnaissance; fire support coordination; logistics and supply
Planning and estimates; radio and telephone service; training and certification; procurement and funding
questions.explanation: Signal Operations organizes support into four categories: command and control communication, cyberspace operations and electronic warfare, repair and maintenance, and recovery and restoration.
