questions.explanation: Synchronization arranges battlefield activities in time and space, using combined arms and mastery of time-space relationships, so every asset is used at the decisive time and place.
why: Depth is fighting throughout the enemy's disposition.
Versatility is flexibility across diverse missions.
Initiative is dictating the terms of battle.

questions.stem: An army brigade detects an imminent enemy buildup along a strategic mountain pass. The commander orders subordinate units to establish fortified holding positions, prepare counter-attack routes, and repel any incoming enemy assaults to protect friendly forces and territory. According to the Elements of Full Spectrum Operations, which type of operation is the brigade primarily executing?
questions.explanation: Defensive operations defeat an enemy attack, gain time, economize forces, and create conditions for later offensive or civil governance operations; fortified positions and repelling assaults fit this.
why: Offensive operations defeat and destroy enemy forces and seize terrain; the brigade here is holding and repelling.
Support to civil governance covers stability and civil support tasks.
Multinational operations is an operational platform about alliance structure, not an element of full spectrum operations.

questions.stem: During a conduct of exercise, a battalion commander synchronizes a group of tasks and systems, including people, organizations, information, and processes united by a common purpose to accomplish the mission. According to the doctrine, what is this group of tasks and systems called?
questions.explanation: Warfighting functions are groups of tasks and systems (people, organizations, information, processes) united by a common purpose that commanders use to accomplish missions.
why: Principles are non-physical factors characterizing successful operations.
Tenets are the five characteristics: initiative, agility, depth, synchronization, versatility.
Full spectrum elements are offensive, defensive and support to civil governance.

questions.stem: Which Army Operational Platform is characterized by the synchronized or simultaneous application of several Army-specific arms (such as infantry, armor, field artillery, engineer, and aviation) to achieve an effect greater than if used separately?
questions.explanation: Combined arms is the synchronized or simultaneous application of several Army arms (infantry, armor, artillery, engineer, aviation) for an effect greater than using them separately.
why: Joint operations involve two or more services under a single commander.
Multinational operations are conducted within an alliance or coalition.
Full spectrum operations are offense, defense and support to civil governance, not a combination of arms.

questions.stem: During a tactical reconnaissance mission, a unit conducts surveillance and reconnaissance operations driven by the commander to facilitate a complete understanding of the operational environment, enemy forces, terrain, and civil considerations. Which Warfighting Function is being applied in this scenario?
questions.explanation: The Intelligence function facilitates understanding of the operational environment, enemy, terrain and civil considerations through commander-driven ISR.
why: Movement and Maneuver moves forces to a position of advantage.
Command and Control supports exercising authority and direction.
Protection preserves the force.

questions.stem: During a night infiltration, a force strikes the enemy at a time, place, and in a manner for which they are completely unprepared, achieving a powerful yet temporary effect. Which principle of Army operations is being applied in this scenario?
questions.explanation: Surprise is striking the enemy at a time, place or manner for which he is unprepared; it is powerful but temporary.
why: Security prevents the enemy from gaining an unexpected advantage.
Simplicity calls for clear, uncomplicated plans.
Mass concentrates combat power at the decisive place and time.

questions.stem: An instructor describes a military concept defined as the summation of potency that a total Army force generates, consisting of warfighting functions tied together by leadership and enhanced by information, representing the total means of destructive, constructive, and information capabilities a formation can apply at a given time. What is being described in this scenario?
questions.explanation: Army Power is the summation of the potency a total Army force generates: warfighting functions tied together by leadership and enhanced by information.
why: Full spectrum operations are offense, defense and support to civil governance.
Warfighting functions are only one component of Army Power.
Principles are non-physical factors of successful operations.

questions.stem: During a combined arms operation, a commander integrates and synchronizes the collective and coordinated use of Army indirect fires, joint fires, and command and control warfare including non-lethal effects through the targeting process to suppress enemy positions. Which warfighting function is being applied in this scenario?
questions.explanation: Fires provides collective and coordinated use of Army indirect fires, joint fires and command and control warfare, including non-lethal effects, through the targeting process.
why: Intelligence supports understanding of the environment and enemy.
Protection preserves the force.
Command and Control supports the commander's direction.

questions.stem: During a tactical engagement, a commander sets the terms of the battle by taking the fight directly to the enemy, maintaining relentless pressure to break their will, and creating a fluid situation where the adversary completely loses control of events. Which tenet of army operations is being applied in this scenario?
questions.explanation: Initiative is setting or dictating the terms of battle by action, taking the fight to the enemy and creating a fluid situation in which the enemy loses control of events.
why: Agility is acting faster than the enemy.
Depth is extending operations in space, time and resources.
Synchronization is massing effects at the decisive point.

questions.stem: According to the doctrine on Army Operational Platforms, what describes "Joint Operations"?
questions.key: Involve forces of two or more services under a single commander.
distractors: Conducted within the structure of an alliance or a coalition.
The synchronized or simultaneous application of several Army-specific arms such as infantry, armor, and field artillery.
Conducted by a single Army unit using only its own organic assets.
questions.explanation: Joint operations bring together forces of two or more services (for example Army, Navy, Air Force) under one commander. It is one of the Army operational platforms, alongside multinational/combined operations and combined arms.
why: This describes multinational or combined operations, which occur within an alliance or coalition.
This is the definition of combined arms, which mixes Army arms rather than separate services.
Joint operations by definition involve two or more services, not a single unit using only organic assets.

questions.stem: An instructor discusses a specific component, noting that it acts as a weapon against the enemy's command and control, serves as a means to affect enemy morale, and is described as both destructive and constructive. Which element of Army Power is being described in this scenario?
questions.explanation: Information is the element of Army Power described as a weapon against enemy command and control and a means to affect enemy morale, both destructive and constructive.
why: Leadership is the multiplying and unifying element, influencing people.
Intelligence facilitates understanding of the environment.
Fires is coordinated use of indirect and joint fires.

questions.stem: During a regional security campaign, an infantry battalion is tasked to secure critical infrastructure, assist local government agencies in disaster response, and conduct community stability projects in a newly liberated municipality. According to Army doctrine, which element of Full Spectrum Operations does this mission primarily fall under?
questions.explanation: Support to civil governance covers missions to maintain or re-establish a safe and secure environment, including disaster response, civil population and vital installation security, and support to community development.
why: Offensive operations are combat actions to defeat and destroy enemy forces and seize terrain.
Defensive operations defeat an enemy attack and gain time; the scenario involves civil support, not defense.
Information operations is a warfighting function, not an element of full spectrum operations.

questions.stem: Which element of Army Power is specifically described as the multiplying and unifying element that is often the difference between success and failure?
questions.explanation: Leadership is the multiplying and unifying element of Army power, often the difference between success and failure; it influences people by providing purpose, direction, and motivation.
why: Information is described as a weapon against enemy command and control, not as the unifying element.
Sustainment provides support and services to extend operational reach and endurance.
Protection preserves the force so the commander can apply maximum Army power.

questions.stem: A company commander wants to ensure that subordinate platoon leaders feel confident to act without constantly waiting for micro-management, knowing that everyone within the unit relies on each other's integrity, professional competence, and shared values. Which principle of Mission Command is the commander primarily building?
questions.explanation: Mutual trust is shared confidence between commanders and subordinates, built through competence, integrity, shared values and leadership by example. It lets subordinates act without waiting for constant direction.
why: Shared understanding is everyone grasping the same mission, environment and priorities, not confidence in one another.
Mission orders state what and why and leave the how to subordinates; they are a tool, not the confidence itself.
Risk acceptance is taking prudent, calculated risk; it does not describe reliance on each other's integrity.

questions.stem: A company commander encourages his soldiers during a difficult operation by expressing confidence in their abilities, sharing a clear vision of success, and boosting their morale to push forward despite challenges. Which component of transformational leadership is being demonstrated?
questions.explanation: Inspirational Motivation is communicating a compelling vision and sense of purpose, expressing confidence and lifting morale so followers push through challenges.
why: Idealized Influence is acting as a role model whose example followers emulate; it is not vision and morale boosting.
Intellectual Stimulation encourages soldiers to question assumptions and innovate; the stem describes encouragement and vision.
Individualized Consideration is coaching each soldier by personal needs; the stem addresses the whole unit.

questions.stem: Which best describes Mutual Trust in Mission Command?
questions.key: Shared confidence between commanders, subordinates, and partners
distractors: A shared picture of the mission, environment, threats, and priorities
Acceptance of calculated hazards to gain a decisive advantage
A statement of purpose, direction, and desired end state
questions.explanation: Mutual trust is the shared confidence between commanders, subordinates and partners. It grows from competence, integrity, shared experience and leadership by example, and it makes initiative possible.
why: That describes Shared Understanding, a different principle of Mission Command.
That describes Risk Acceptance, the willingness to take prudent, calculated risk.
That describes Commander's Intent, not trust.

questions.stem: Halfway through a multi-day field training exercise, a signal company suffers an abrupt, total communications blackout due to heavy atmospheric interference. Instead of panicking or assigning blame to the radio operators, the company commander keeps a level head, directs the team to shift immediately to backup tactical procedures, and oversees the recovery. Which attribute is demonstrated?
questions.key: Resilience by recovering from setbacks and adapting to adversity under pressure
distractors: Discipline through consistent behavior, lawful order enforcement, and standard compliance
Empathy by seeing a situation from a subordinate's point of view and caring about their feelings
Innovation by introducing a new method or creative idea to challenge subordinates
questions.explanation: Resilience is the psychological and physical capacity to recover quickly from setbacks, shock and stress. Staying calm, shifting to backup procedures and overseeing recovery after the blackout shows it.
why: Discipline is about enforcing standards and orders; no standards violation occurs in this scenario.
Empathy is understanding others' feelings; the scenario is about recovering from a setback.
Innovation is introducing something new; the commander uses existing backup procedures.

questions.stem: Which of the following is considered one of the most important leadership situations that an NCO may face?
questions.key: Leading soldiers during combat or high-risk operations
questions.explanation: Combat and other high-risk operations place the greatest demand on an NCO because soldiers' lives and the mission depend on his leadership. Course notes also stress assuming a leadership position as a key leadership situation.
why: A routine inventory is a normal administrative duty, not a defining leadership situation.
Leave and pay paperwork is administrative support, not one of an NCO's most important leadership situations.
Ceremonies are routine events and do not test leadership the way combat does.

questions.stem: Which leadership style involves a leader working with followers beyond their self-interests to create a vision, inspire change, and guide transformation through influence and commitment?
questions.explanation: Transformational leadership works with followers beyond self-interest to build a vision, inspire change and guide it through influence and commitment.
why: Transactional leadership is an exchange of effort for reward or correction, not vision and change.
Laissez-faire leadership is hands-off and offers no vision or guidance.
Autocratic leadership relies on the leader's own control rather than shared commitment.

questions.stem: An NCO enforces standards of military appearance, so he corrects soldiers who wear the uniform improperly and teaches the standard. What type of responsibility does this best demonstrate?
questions.explanation: Command responsibility is collective, organizational accountability for how well the unit performs and maintains standards. Enforcing uniform and appearance standards across the unit falls under it.
why: Supply responsibility concerns equipment accountability, not uniform standards.
Judicial responsibility concerns punishment and protecting soldiers' rights, not correcting appearance.
Combat responsibility concerns fighting and tactical duties, not wear of the uniform.

questions.stem: A company leader takes time to understand each soldier's strengths, weaknesses, and personal needs, and provides guidance and support tailored to help them improve and succeed in their duties. Which component of transformational leadership is being demonstrated?
questions.explanation: Individualized Consideration is coaching and mentoring each soldier according to personal strengths, weaknesses and needs.
why: Inspirational Motivation is about vision and purpose for the group, not tailored guidance.
Idealized Influence is role-modelling, not personalized support.
Intellectual Stimulation challenges soldiers to question assumptions and innovate, not to meet personal needs.

questions.stem: A company commander issues an operation order that clearly outlines the purpose of the operation, the key tasks, and the desired end state, allowing subordinates to understand the ultimate goal even if the original plan completely breaks down. What element of Mission Command is this?
questions.explanation: Commander's intent gives purpose, key tasks and the desired end state, so subordinates can keep acting toward the goal when the plan breaks down.
why: Competence is the professional skill of leaders; it does not supply the purpose and end state.
Mutual trust is shared confidence; it does not state the goal of the operation.
Risk acceptance is taking prudent risk; it is not a statement of purpose.

questions.stem: A company commander discovers during a routine supply inventory that several sensitive items are unaccounted for. A subordinate suggests quietly writing off the missing gear as "administrative error" to prevent the battalion commander from lowering the company's operational rating. The commander refuses and immediately reports the discrepancy with an initiated investigation plan. Which leadership attribute is the commander primarily demonstrating?
questions.key: Applying the moral foundation of Army values to decisions, actions, and relationships
distractors: Resilience by recovering from setbacks and adapting to adversity under pressure
Innovation by introducing a new method or creative idea to improve the unit
Mental agility by flexibly adapting thinking to uncertain or changing situations
questions.explanation: Refusing to hide the shortage and reporting it with an investigation plan puts Army values (honor and integrity) above self-interest and the unit's rating. That is the moral foundation of character.
why: Resilience is recovering from setbacks; no setback or recovery is described.
Innovation is introducing something new; the commander is acting honestly, not creatively.
Mental agility is flexibility of mind; the issue here is honesty, not adaptation.

questions.stem: Which of the following goes beyond mere tasks and encompasses a broader sense of obligation or accountability?
questions.explanation: Responsibilities go beyond tasks to a broader sense of obligation or accountability for soldiers' welfare, standards, regulations and mission results.
why: Duties are the specific tasks or assignments, the narrower concept.
Authority is the legitimate power to command and enforce obedience, not accountability.
Commandership is applying leadership, management and command to authority, not general accountability.

questions.stem: Which scenario exemplifies Inspirational Motivation?
questions.key: Giving routine standards a deeper purpose by explaining how they protect teammates.
distractors: Setting a personal example by following standards even when no one is watching.
Asking soldiers to challenge a procedure and propose a better way.
Privately mentoring a soldier and adjusting duties during a personal crisis.
questions.explanation: Inspirational Motivation gives ordinary tasks meaning by communicating purpose. Explaining how a standard protects teammates ties the routine to a shared mission.
why: That is Idealized Influence, leading by example.
That is Intellectual Stimulation, inviting questioning and innovation.
That is Individualized Consideration, personal coaching and support.

questions.stem: Which of the following best demonstrates a leader's presence?
questions.key: A leader maintains a professional appearance and confidently engages with subordinates during unit activities.
distractors: A leader accurately reports a discrepancy and starts corrective action despite pressure.
A leader studies doctrine to assess a situation and reach a sound decision.
A leader privately listens to a soldier's family problem and shows understanding.
questions.explanation: Presence is the image a leader projects. A professional appearance and confident engagement with soldiers show military bearing and confidence.
why: That shows integrity, an aspect of Character, not Presence.
That shows Intellect (judgment and knowledge).
That shows empathy, part of Character.

questions.stem: A company commander consistently maintains personal COMSEC discipline and models high standards of integrity so that subordinates follow the example rather than just an order. Which leadership competency category under "A CO must lead" does this best demonstrate?
questions.explanation: Displaying character and demonstrating competence by personal example, such as keeping COMSEC discipline and integrity, is what the leads-by-example competency covers.
why: Prepares self is a "develop" competency about the commander's own readiness.
Stewards the profession is a "develop" competency, not part of leading.
Creates a positive environment is a "develop" competency about unit climate.

questions.stem: Which situation best demonstrates effective communication?
questions.key: A leader ensures instructions are clearly understood before execution
distractors: A leader issues orders quickly and moves on without seeking feedback.
A leader relays instructions only in writing to avoid questions.
A leader gives information only to key staff so subordinates are not confused.
questions.explanation: Effective communication includes ensuring shared understanding. Confirming instructions are understood before execution prevents mistakes and builds unity of effort.
why: Skipping feedback leaves misunderstanding unchecked.
Avoiding questions blocks confirmation of understanding.
Withholding information undermines shared understanding.

questions.stem: Moral and ethical quality of a leader that helps determine what is right and gives a motivation to do what is appropriate.
questions.explanation: Leader character is the moral and ethical quality that determines what is right and motivates a leader to do it. It includes Army core values, empathy and Warrior Ethos.
why: Presence is the image a leader projects.
Intellect is the mental tendencies shaping conceptual abilities.
Military Leadership Attributes is the whole set that includes character, not the moral quality itself.

questions.stem: A company commander decides to use a faster, less secure mountain trail to achieve tactical surprise against an insurgent camp, accepting the calculated hazard of rough terrain and reduced communication in exchange for a decisive tactical advantage. Which principle of Mission Command is the commander applying?
questions.explanation: Risk acceptance means taking prudent, calculated risk to gain advantage. The commander knowingly takes a rough trail for tactical surprise.
why: Competence is professional skill, not accepting hazard.
Mutual trust is confidence between leaders, not trading hazard for advantage.
Shared understanding is a common picture of the mission.

questions.stem: Which action best demonstrates Idealized Influence at the unit level?
questions.key: Adhering strictly to COMSEC protocols personally when no one is watching.
distractors: Explaining to soldiers how a routine standard protects their teammates.
Encouraging soldiers to challenge an existing procedure and propose a better one.
Offering a reward to soldiers when they meet a performance target.
questions.explanation: Idealized Influence is leading by example. Personally keeping COMSEC even when unobserved makes the leader a role model who earns followership.
why: That is Inspirational Motivation, giving purpose.
That is Intellectual Stimulation.
That is a transactional exchange, not role modelling.

questions.stem: Before launching a night insertion, a company commander gathers all platoon leaders and key NCOs to brief the operational environment, the enemy situation, and the purpose of the maneuver until every leader clearly visualizes the same operational picture. Which principle of Mission Command is being established?
questions.explanation: Shared understanding means leaders all grasp the mission, environment, threats and priorities. Briefing everyone until they see the same picture builds it.
why: Competence is leader skill, not a common picture.
Risk acceptance is taking prudent risk.
Disciplined initiative is acting without orders within intent.

questions.stem: Which leadership style focuses on the exchange of skills, knowledge, resources, or effort between leaders and subordinates?
questions.explanation: Transactional leadership is an exchange between leader and followers of effort, resources or skills for reward or correction.
why: Transformational leadership inspires change beyond self-interest rather than exchange.
Laissez-faire leaders give little direction and no exchange.
Autocratic leaders command without an exchange of effort and reward.

questions.stem: Which of the following refers to the specific tasks or assignments that individuals within the Philippine Army are expected to perform?
questions.explanation: Duties are the specific tasks or assignments individuals in the Army are expected to perform.
why: Responsibilities go beyond tasks to broader accountability.
Authority is the legitimate right to command.
Command responsibility is collective accountability for unit performance.

questions.stem: A company commander dedicates personal time to study military doctrine, evaluate their own leadership performance, and maintain professional readiness. Which specific competency is the commander demonstrating?
questions.explanation: Prepares self covers a commander's own study of doctrine, self-evaluation and readiness for new challenges.
why: Develops leaders focuses on mentoring others.
Creates a positive environment concerns unit climate.
Builds trust is a leading competency about relationships.

questions.stem: A leader organizes resources, sets clear goals, and ensures tasks are completed efficiently to meet mission objectives. Which competency is being demonstrated?
questions.explanation: Achieving is getting results: organizing resources, setting clear goals and completing tasks to meet mission objectives.
why: Leading is influencing and guiding people.
Developing builds individuals and the organization.
Leads by example is a subset of leading, not goal accomplishment.

questions.stem: Which scenario represents Individualized Consideration?
questions.key: Privately mentoring a soldier and adjusting duties during a personal crisis.
distractors: Giving routine standards a deeper purpose by explaining how they protect teammates.
Encouraging soldiers to question assumptions and propose better ways.
Modeling high standards so soldiers want to follow, not just obey.
questions.explanation: Individualized Consideration is personal coaching and support. Mentoring privately and adjusting duties during a crisis fits each soldier's needs.
why: That is Inspirational Motivation.
That is Intellectual Stimulation.
That is Idealized Influence.

questions.stem: Core leader competencies focus on who is being led and with what degree of authority and influence.
questions.explanation: The Leading Competency focuses on who is being led and with what authority and influence, and addresses how leaders convey influence.
why: Developing competency is about improving self, others and the organization.
Achieving competency is about accomplishing the mission.
Leaders Presence is an attribute, not a core competency.

questions.stem: Instead of dictating every minute step of how a platoon must secure a designated crossroads, a company commander issues a directive stating what needs to be done and why, while leaving the how entirely up to the platoon leader's tactical judgment. What element of Mission Command is being utilized?
questions.explanation: Mission orders tell subordinates what is to be done and why, leaving the how to their judgment, emphasizing results over methods.
why: Competence is skill, not the style of directive.
Mutual trust is confidence between leaders.
Shared understanding is a common picture of the situation.

questions.stem: The regulation of forces and war fighting functions to accomplish the mission in accordance with the commander's intent.
questions.explanation: Control is the regulation of forces and warfighting functions to accomplish the mission in accordance with the commander's intent.
why: Command is the authority and direction, not regulation.
Shared understanding is a Mission Command principle.
Competence is leader skill.

questions.stem: According to the Warrior Ethos, which statement best demonstrates unrelenting and consistent determination to do what is right, perform duties with pride, and sustain the will to win?
questions.key: A soldier continues to accomplish the mission despite fatigue, adversity, and obstacles while maintaining professional standards.
distractors: A soldier requests relief from the task once fatigue sets in to preserve comfort.
A soldier waits for explicit orders before acting on any unexpected development.
A soldier follows minimum standards only while being supervised.
questions.explanation: Warrior Ethos requires unrelenting, consistent determination to do what is right with pride and to sustain the will to win. Continuing the mission despite hardship shows it.
why: Quitting for comfort contradicts the will to win.
Waiting for orders is a lack of initiative, not determination.
Standards only under supervision are not consistent determination.

questions.stem: Consist of the principles, standards, and qualities considered essential for successful Army leaders.
questions.explanation: Army core values are the principles, standards and qualities essential for successful Army leaders: Honor, Patriotism and Duty.
why: Warrior Ethos is the determination to do right and sustain the will to win.
Empathy is seeing things from another's point of view.
Presence is the image the leader projects.

questions.stem: A company commander takes time to understand how their team perceives a stressful situation, respects individual differences within the squad, and maintains composure under pressure. What attribute or skill does this best demonstrate?
questions.explanation: Interpersonal tact is knowing what others perceive, recognizing diversity and displaying self-control, which this commander shows.
why: Mental agility is flexibility of mind in changing situations.
Sound judgment is assessing situations to reach feasible conclusions.
Innovation is introducing something new.

questions.stem: During a demanding field training exercise, which action best reflects resilience in a soldier?
questions.key: A soldier maintains focus and continues performing assigned duties after recovering from a challenging setback during an operation.
distractors: A soldier asks to be replaced after a setback to avoid further stress.
A soldier keeps a sharp uniform and projects authority during formation.
A soldier stays physically fit before deployment to endure stress.
questions.explanation: Resilience is recovering quickly from setbacks. Staying focused and carrying on duties after a setback shows it.
why: Asking to be replaced is the opposite of recovering.
That shows military bearing.
That shows health and physical fitness.

questions.stem: During a tactical movement exercise, a company commander notices a soldier repeatedly violating standard operating safety procedures by failing to secure weapon lines. Instead of losing his temper or ignoring it because the soldier is a top athlete, the leader calmly halts the movement, addresses the infraction strictly by the book, and implements standard corrective training. Which leadership attribute is being exhibited?
questions.key: Discipline through consistent behavior, lawful order enforcement, and standard compliance
distractors: Resilience by recovering from setbacks and adapting to adversity under pressure
Empathy by seeing a situation from a subordinate's point of view
Innovation by introducing a new method or creative idea
questions.explanation: Discipline is consistent, fair enforcement of standards. The commander halts movement, addresses the violation by the book and applies corrective training.
why: Resilience is recovery from setbacks; none occurs.
Empathy is understanding another's feelings.
Innovation is introducing something new; he applies existing standards.

questions.stem: Leadership style that focuses on the exchange of skills, knowledge, resources, or effort between leaders and their subordinates.
questions.explanation: Transactional leadership is an exchange of skills, knowledge, resources or effort between leader and subordinates.
why: Transformational leadership inspires beyond self-interest.
Laissez-faire leaders do not exchange; they stay hands-off.
Autocratic leaders issue directives without exchange.

questions.stem: A company commander guides soldiers, applies authority appropriately, and influences them to accomplish the mission effectively. Which competency is being demonstrated?
questions.explanation: Leading is guiding soldiers, applying authority and influencing them toward the mission.
why: Achieving is accomplishing results with resources.
Developing is building people and the organization.
Prepares self is the commander's own readiness.

questions.stem: It will lead you to apply not only leadership, but also management and command and apply these to authority.
questions.explanation: Commandership combines leadership, management and command applied to authority. The commander practices the art of command.
why: Followership is the role of subordinates.
Mentorship is guiding juniors.
Stewardship is caring for resources or the profession.

questions.stem: A company commander takes deliberate steps to cultivate mutual respect, stamp out toxic climates, and foster a healthy organizational culture within the unit. Which competency under "A CO must develop" does this action best represent?
questions.explanation: Creates a positive environment means cultivating mutual respect, a healthy culture and removing toxic climates. It is a "develop" competency.
why: Develops leaders is mentoring.
Prepares self is own readiness.
Builds trust is a "lead" competency, not under develop.

questions.stem: During a patrol, a platoon leader encounters an unexpected enemy observation post that threatens the company's flank, a situation not explicitly covered in the original operations order. Instead of halting to ask for permission, the platoon leader aggressively maneuvers to neutralize the threat based on the previously understood company objective. What element of Mission Command does this action demonstrate?
questions.explanation: Disciplined initiative is acting independently to solve problems within the commander's intent when the plan does not cover a situation.
why: Mutual trust is the confidence enabling initiative, not the act itself.
Shared understanding is the common picture.
Risk acceptance is taking prudent risk; the stem stresses acting without waiting.

questions.stem: During a high-stakes nighttime tactical displacement, the lead element reports that a sudden civilian blockade completely severs the designated primary axis of advance. Rather than showing hesitation or repeatedly querying higher headquarters for instructions, the company commander evaluates alternative routes on the map, projects a calm and steady demeanor, and issues authoritative redirection vectors to the platoon leaders over the net, ensuring zero panic ripples through the formation. Which specific leadership attribute is the commander primarily demonstrating?
questions.key: Confidence through self-assurance and steady composure when executing command responsibilities during unforeseen crises
distractors: Applying the moral foundation of Army values to decisions, actions, and relationships
Empathy by seeing a situation from a subordinate's point of view
Innovation by introducing a new method or creative idea
questions.explanation: Confidence is projecting self-assurance and steady composure. The commander stays calm and decisive during the crisis and prevents panic.
why: That describes integrity, not composure.
Empathy is understanding another's feelings.
Innovation is introducing something new.

questions.stem: A company commander mentors junior leaders, provides training opportunities, and ensures that their skills are improved so the unit becomes more capable over time. Which competency is being demonstrated?
questions.explanation: Developing is mentoring, training and improving subordinates so the unit grows more capable.
why: Leading is guiding and influencing people.
Achieving is accomplishing tasks.
Extends influence is a leading subset outside the chain of command.

questions.stem: A company commander consistently demonstrates honesty, fairness, and accountability in decision-making. As a result, soldiers respect their leader and remain motivated even during difficult missions. What is the primary benefit of ethical leadership in this situation?
questions.key: Enhances trust, discipline, and morale among troops
distractors: Reduces the need for training and supervision of soldiers
Guarantees mission success regardless of enemy action
Replaces the need for formal standards and regulations
questions.explanation: Ethical leadership builds trust, discipline and morale because soldiers respect honest, fair, accountable leaders.
why: Ethics does not remove the need for training.
No leadership style guarantees success.
Ethics supports standards; it does not replace them.

questions.stem: A leadership style where a leader works with teams/followers beyond their immediate self-interests to identify needed change, creating a vision to guide the change through influence, inspiration, and executing the change in tandem with committed members of a group.
questions.explanation: Transformational leadership works beyond self-interest to identify change, create a vision and execute it with committed followers.
why: Transactional leadership is exchange.
Laissez-faire leadership is hands-off.
Autocratic leadership is directive.

questions.stem: Which of the following best demonstrates Idealized Influence (Charisma)?
questions.key: A leader sets a strong personal example through integrity, confidence, and high standards that earns respect and trust.
distractors: Communicating a compelling vision and explaining the purpose behind the mission.
Encouraging soldiers to question assumptions and innovate on problems.
Coaching and mentoring each soldier according to individual needs and potential.
questions.explanation: Idealized Influence is being a role model. Personal integrity, confidence and high standards earn respect and trust.
why: That is Inspirational Motivation.
That is Intellectual Stimulation.
That is Individualized Consideration.

questions.stem: Aims at using these existing qualities and potential to develop a well-rounded leader with sets of desired attributes forming the leader's character, presence, and intellect.
questions.explanation: Military leadership attributes are the qualities that form a well-rounded leader: character, presence and intellect.
why: Competencies are what leaders do: lead, develop, achieve.
Army core values are only part of character.
Warrior Ethos is part of character.

questions.stem: During a field exercise, a company commander insists on transparently reporting a compliance error rather than covering it up, which is crucial for maintaining trust, discipline, and morale among troops. What concept does this best demonstrate?
questions.explanation: Ethical leadership is leading by honesty and accountability, such as transparently reporting errors, which preserves trust, discipline and morale.
why: Transactional leadership is exchange.
Commandership is the art of command.
Domain knowledge is an Intellect component.

questions.stem: A company commander actively mentors junior officers, coaches subordinates through professional challenges, and ensures future leaders are prepared to step up. Under which major grouping of company commander competencies does this fall?
questions.explanation: Mentoring junior officers and preparing future leaders falls under "A CO must develop," along with preparing self and creating a positive environment.
why: "Lead" covers leading others and influence.
"Achieve" covers mission accomplishment.
"Administer" is not a competency group.

questions.stem: Which behavior best demonstrates military and professional bearing?
questions.key: Maintaining proper uniform standards, military courtesy, punctuality, and professional conduct.
distractors: Remaining calm and recovering quickly after a setback during an operation.
Accurately reporting a discrepancy and initiating corrective action.
Keeping physically fit and ensuring soldiers get rest and medical care.
questions.explanation: Military and professional bearing means a commanding, professional image: correct uniform worn with pride, courtesy, punctuality and proper conduct.
why: That describes resilience, a different Presence component.
That describes integrity, part of Character.
That describes health and physical fitness, another Presence component.

questions.stem: Two platoon leaders disagree about the allocation of communications equipment. Which action best demonstrates interpersonal tact?
questions.key: Listen to both leaders, consider their requirements, and explain the decision respectfully.
distractors: Decide immediately in favor of the senior leader without hearing the other side.
Allocate the equipment by rank and tell both leaders to stop arguing.
Avoid the issue and let the leaders settle it between themselves.
questions.explanation: Interpersonal tact is knowing what others perceive, recognizing different views and keeping self-control. Hearing both leaders and explaining the decision respectfully shows it.
why: Ignoring one side disregards others' perceptions.
Dismissing both leaders shows no recognition of their needs.
Avoiding the problem leaves the dispute unresolved and shows no leadership.

questions.stem: What is Intellect as a military leadership attribute?
questions.key: The mental abilities and knowledge that enable a leader to understand situations, make sound decisions, and solve problems.
distractors: The leader's moral and ethical qualities that guide decisions and actions.
The impression a leader makes through appearance, demeanor, actions, and words.
The process of influencing, motivating, and directing soldiers to accomplish the mission while improving the organization.
questions.explanation: Intellect draws on the mental tendencies and resources that shape a leader's conceptual abilities: mental agility, sound judgment, innovation, interpersonal tact and domain knowledge.
why: That describes Character.
That describes Presence.
That is the definition of military leadership, not an attribute.

questions.stem: Which statement best explains how Character, Presence, and Intellect work together?
questions.key: Character guides ethical conduct, Presence inspires confidence, and Intellect enables informed decisions and effective solutions.
distractors: Character inspires confidence, Presence guides ethical conduct, and Intellect enables informed decisions and effective solutions.
Character enables informed decisions, Presence guides ethical conduct, and Intellect inspires confidence.
The three attributes work independently, so a leader needs strength in only one of them.
questions.explanation: Character supplies moral and ethical guidance, Presence is the image that inspires confidence, and Intellect supplies the thinking for sound decisions. Together they form a well-rounded leader.
why: It swaps the roles of Character and Presence.
It misassigns all three roles.
The attributes are complementary; they are meant to be developed together.

questions.stem: A soldier's performance declines because of a serious family problem. What should a platoon leader do to demonstrate empathy?
questions.key: Privately discuss the situation, arrange appropriate assistance, and maintain mission requirements.
distractors: Discuss the problem openly in formation so peers can offer support.
Ignore the problem and apply the same standards to maintain fairness.
Relieve the soldier of all duties until the problem is resolved.
questions.explanation: Empathy is seeing things from another's point of view and caring for the soldier and family. Discussing it privately, arranging help and still keeping the mission shows empathy without neglecting duty.
why: Public discussion embarrasses the soldier and ignores privacy.
Ignoring the problem shows no empathy.
Relieving all duties disregards mission requirements and is not a balanced response.

questions.stem: During a field exercise, the primary radio system fails. The commander remains composed, implements contingency procedures, and coordinates restoration. Which Presence component is most clearly demonstrated?
questions.explanation: Resilience is the capacity to recover quickly from setbacks, shock and stress. Staying composed, using contingency procedures and restoring service shows it.
why: Bearing concerns uniform, courtesy and professional image.
Fitness concerns physical and mental conditioning.
Mental agility is an Intellect component, not Presence.

questions.stem: What does Presence primarily describe?
questions.key: The impression a leader makes through appearance, demeanor, actions, and words.
distractors: The leader's moral and ethical qualities that guide decisions and actions.
The mental abilities and knowledge that enable a leader to understand situations, make sound decisions, and solve problems.
The process of influencing, motivating, and directing soldiers to accomplish the mission while improving the organization.
questions.explanation: Presence is a matter of showing up: the image the leader projects through appearance, demeanor, actions and words. It includes bearing, fitness, confidence and resilience.
why: That describes Character.
That describes Intellect.
That is the definition of military leadership.

questions.stem: Two platoon leaders disagree about the allocation of communications equipment. Which action best demonstrates interpersonal tact?
questions.key: Listen to both leaders, consider their requirements, and explain the decision respectfully.
distractors: Decide immediately in favor of the senior leader without hearing the other side.
Allocate the equipment by rank and tell both leaders to stop arguing.
Avoid the issue and let the leaders settle it between themselves.
questions.explanation: Interpersonal tact is knowing what others perceive, recognizing different views and keeping self-control. Hearing both leaders and explaining the decision respectfully shows it.
why: Ignoring one side disregards others' perceptions.
Dismissing both leaders shows no recognition of their needs.
Avoiding the problem leaves the dispute unresolved and shows no leadership.

questions.stem: Which of the following correctly identifies the three military leadership attributes?
questions.explanation: The three military leadership attributes are Character, Presence and Intellect.
why: Competence and Commitment are not the attribute categories.
Honor, Patriotism and Duty are the Army core values under Character.
Leading, Developing and Achieving are the core leader competencies.

questions.stem: An unexpected operational change requires a company commander to revise the movement plan. Which action best demonstrates confidence?
questions.key: Calmly assess the situation, consult subordinate leaders when appropriate, and issue clear instructions.
distractors: Delay any decision until higher headquarters provides complete guidance.
Keep the original plan and ignore the change to avoid appearing uncertain.
Pass the decision to subordinate leaders and avoid issuing instructions.
questions.explanation: Confidence helps leaders and soldiers control doubt in uncertain situations. Calmly assessing, consulting where appropriate and giving clear instructions shows it.
why: Waiting for full guidance shows hesitation.
Ignoring the change is rigid and disregards the situation.
Avoiding instructions abandons the leader's responsibility.

questions.stem: During a prolonged field exercise, which action best demonstrates fitness as a leadership attribute?
questions.key: Maintaining personal readiness while ensuring appropriate rest, hydration, and medical attention for soldiers.
distractors: Continue operations nonstop to show endurance, regardless of soldiers' condition.
Focus only on personal fitness and leave soldiers to arrange their own rest.
Skip rest and meals to set an example while ignoring medical concerns.
questions.explanation: Health and physical fitness mean a leader keeps personal readiness and ensures soldiers' rest, hydration and medical care, because stress compromises mental and emotional fitness.
why: Nonstop operations ignore soldiers' limits.
Leaving soldiers' welfare unaddressed neglects the leader's role.
Ignoring medical concerns undermines readiness.

questions.stem: A commander receives conflicting reports about the condition of a bridge. What action best demonstrates sound judgment?
questions.key: Evaluate the available information, verify the bridge's condition, and determine whether crossing is safe.
distractors: Trust the first report received and order the crossing immediately.
Order the crossing and rely on soldiers to report problems as they occur.
Cancel the mission entirely without checking either report.
questions.explanation: Sound judgment is assessing situations to draw feasible conclusions. Weighing the reports and verifying the bridge before crossing does this.
why: Relying on the first report ignores the conflict.
Crossing first risks lives and equipment.
Canceling unverified is not a judgment based on facts.

questions.stem: During an equipment inventory, a company commander discovers missing equipment. Which action best demonstrates integrity?
questions.key: Accurately report the discrepancy and initiate corrective action.
distractors: Quietly adjust the records so the shortage does not appear in the inventory.
Wait to see whether the equipment turns up before telling anyone.
Publicly blame the supply sergeant without investigating.
questions.explanation: Integrity, part of Character and the Army values, means being honest and accountable. Accurately reporting the discrepancy and starting corrective action shows it.
why: Altering records is dishonest.
Delaying the report hides the problem.
Blaming without investigation is unfair and avoids accountability.

questions.stem: Which statement is NOT part of the Warrior Ethos presented in the lesson?
questions.key: Always prioritize personal comfort over mission accomplishment.
distractors: Maintain unrelenting and consistent determination to do what is right and do it with pride.
questions.explanation: The Warrior Ethos calls for unrelenting determination to do right with pride and to sustain the will to win. Putting personal comfort above the mission contradicts it, so that statement is the one that does not belong.
why: This is part of the Warrior Ethos, so it is not the exception.
Sustaining the will to win is part of the Warrior Ethos.
Putting the mission first is consistent with the Warrior Ethos.

questions.stem: A signal company commander applies knowledge of radio communications, network operations, communications security, and equipment limitations to resolve technical problems. Which component is demonstrated?
questions.explanation: Expertise is the technical and professional knowledge a leader applies to a task. Using knowledge of radios, networks and COMSEC to solve problems shows it. The lesson names this intellect component domain knowledge; the exam keyed it as Expertise.
why: Innovation is introducing something new.
Mental agility is adapting to changing situations.
Sound judgment is assessing situations to reach conclusions.

questions.stem: A signal company experiences repeated delays in reporting equipment failures. The commander introduces a standardized digital reporting system. Which Intellect component is demonstrated?
questions.explanation: Innovation is the ability to introduce something new. A standardized digital reporting system is a new way of solving a recurring problem.
why: Mental agility is adapting to uncertain or changing situations.
Sound judgment is assessing a situation to reach a conclusion.
Interpersonal tact is dealing with people's perceptions and showing self-control.

questions.stem: What is the primary focus of Character as a military leadership attribute?
questions.key: The leader's moral and ethical qualities that guide decisions and actions.
distractors: The impression a leader makes through appearance, demeanor, actions, and words.
The mental abilities and knowledge that enable a leader to understand situations, make sound decisions, and solve problems.
The psychological and physical capacity to recover quickly from setbacks and stress.
questions.explanation: Character is the leader's moral and ethical quality that helps determine what is right and motivates doing it. It includes Army core values, empathy and the Warrior Ethos.
why: That describes Presence.
That describes Intellect.
That describes resilience, a Presence component.

questions.stem: A soldier violates an established safety procedure during an operation. Which response best demonstrates discipline?
questions.key: Apply standards fairly, address the violation, and conduct corrective training.
distractors: Overlook the violation if the soldier is otherwise a high performer.
Punish the soldier harshly in front of the unit to deter others.
Report the violation upward and leave all corrective action to someone else.
questions.explanation: Discipline is consistent, fair standard enforcement. Applying standards fairly, addressing the violation and conducting corrective training fits it.
why: Overlooking the violation is inconsistent.
Harsh public punishment is not fair, standard-based correction.
Passing it upward avoids the leader's duty to correct.

questions.stem: A company commander discovers that the planned movement route is impassable because of flooding. The commander assesses alternative routes and adjusts the plan. Which Intellect component is demonstrated?
questions.explanation: Mental agility is flexibility of mind, anticipating or adapting to uncertain or changing situations. Assessing alternative routes and adjusting the plan shows it.
why: Interpersonal tact deals with people and diversity.
Expertise is technical knowledge, not adapting.
Empathy is a Character component.

questions.stem: What is military leadership?
questions.key: The process of influencing, motivating, and directing soldiers to accomplish the mission while improving the organization.
distractors: The authority to give orders and enforce obedience within the military hierarchy.
The regulation of forces and warfighting functions to accomplish the mission.
The legally established obligation a soldier assumes for his own actions.
questions.explanation: Military leadership is influencing, motivating and directing soldiers to accomplish the mission while improving the organization.
why: That describes authority.
That describes control.
That describes responsibility.

questions.stem: It is a task that must be performed to successfully accomplish a specified or essential task, even though it is not explicitly directed in the order or mission statement.
questions.explanation: An implied task is not written in the order but must be done to carry out a specified task. It is found by analyzing the order, enemy, terrain, civil considerations and doctrinal requirements.
why: A specified task is stated outright in the order or mission statement, so it is the opposite of unstated.
An essential task is a specified or implied task that must be done to accomplish the mission; it is not defined by being unstated.
A constraint is a limit on freedom of action (what you cannot or must do), not a task to be performed.

questions.stem: A command post requires real-time analysis of troop movements, weather updates, and logistic statuses. Which sub-system provides this capability for effective decision-making?
questions.explanation: The information system is the C4S sub-system that collects, processes, analyzes and presents data (movements, weather, logistics) so the commander can decide in real time.
why: The communications system conveys information between points; it does not do the analysis and processing described.
The electronics system covers electronic equipment and non-communications emitters, not the processing of information for decisions.
Visual signaling is a simple means of sending pre-arranged messages, not an analysis capability.

questions.stem: What means of signal communications interconnect closely located activities?
questions.explanation: Wire and cable systems physically link nearby stations and facilities, such as command post elements, by direct line.
why: Messengers carry written or oral messages by person; they are not a cable interconnection.
Visual signals pass pre-arranged messages by sight and do not physically interconnect activities.
Satellite links serve long-distance, beyond line-of-sight needs rather than closely located activities.

questions.stem: What is a facility that encompasses the personnel and equipment necessary to provide signal communications by any particular means or combination thereof?
questions.explanation: An agency of communications is the facility, with its people and equipment, that provides signal communications by one or a combination of means (for example a message center or signal center).
why: A means of communications is the medium by which a message is conveyed, not the facility that houses people and equipment.
A radio net is an organization of stations sharing a frequency, not a facility.
A signal is the method of conveying information, not the facility providing it.

questions.stem: Crucial for maintaining trust, discipline, and morale among troops.
questions.explanation: Ethical leadership, leading by right example and sound moral standards, is what sustains trust, discipline and morale among troops.
why: Innovation is the leader's ability to introduce something new, not the source of trust and discipline.
Interpersonal tact is perceiving others and showing self-control; it is a skill, not the ethical foundation described.
Doctrine is the authoritative guide on how the Army fights; it is not a leadership quality.

questions.stem: Consist of the principles, standards, and qualities considered essential for successful Army leaders.
questions.explanation: Army core values are the principles, standards and qualities essential for successful Army leaders: Honor, Patriotism and Duty.
why: Warrior Ethos is the determination to do right and sustain the will to win.
Empathy is seeing things from another's point of view.
Presence is the image the leader projects.

questions.stem: Maybe received in the form of either a written or oral warning order, operation order (OPORD) or Fragmentary Order (FRAGO).
questions.explanation: Receipt of mission is the first step of MDMP/TLP: the unit receives the mission as a warning order, OPORD or FRAGO, written or oral.
why: Mission analysis follows receipt; it studies the received mission rather than being how it arrives.
COA development comes after mission analysis, when options are built.
COA analysis (war game) tests developed courses of action and comes later.

questions.stem: While preparing for a large-scale exercise, a commander organizes his units according to key areas such as movement, fires, and intelligence. What concept is being applied to align unit capabilities with training objectives?
questions.explanation: The warfighting functions (such as movement and maneuver, fires, intelligence) group related unit capabilities and tasks so they can be aligned with objectives.
why: The principles of war are broad guidelines for conducting war, not a way to group capabilities by function.
Troop leading procedure is the process leaders use to receive a mission, plan and execute it.
A signal estimate is a signal staff analysis for communications planning, not a grouping of capabilities.

questions.stem: Describes the Army leader's ability to introduce something new.
questions.explanation: Innovation is the leader's ability to introduce something new, such as a new idea or method, when current ones do not fit the problem.
why: Interpersonal tact is perceiving others' views and keeping self-control, not creating something new.
Ethics concerns moral standards of conduct, not introducing new ideas.
Warrior ethos is the will to win and to do what is right, not creativity.

questions.stem: Results from collecting, locating, processing, analyzing, and reporting intercepted communications and non-communications emitters.
questions.explanation: SIGINT is intelligence derived from intercepted communications and non-communications emitters (COMINT, ELINT), through collection, processing, analysis and reporting.
why: IMINT comes from imagery such as photos, video and radar imagery, not from intercepted emissions.
HUMINT comes from human sources such as informants and interrogations.
MASINT comes from measuring technical signatures of targets, not from intercepting emitters.

questions.stem: What are all measures taken to protect all information which may be of value to the enemy or to deliberately mislead the enemy in the interpretation of information they may gather?
questions.explanation: COMSEC covers all measures to protect information of value to the enemy and to deny the enemy accurate interpretation of what he gathers, such as codes, authentication and transmission security.
why: SIGINT is collection by intercepting emissions; it is collection, not protection.
IMINT is intelligence from imagery, an intelligence discipline rather than a protective measure.
HUMINT is intelligence from human sources, not a security measure.

questions.stem: The dynamic process by which a commander receives a mission, plans it and executes it.
questions.explanation: Troop leading procedure (and MDMP for larger staffs) is the dynamic process by which a commander receives a mission, plans it and executes it.
why: A signal estimate is a staff analysis of communications support, not the whole receive-plan-execute process.
A running estimate is a continuously updated staff assessment within the process, not the process itself.
A warning order is one product issued during the process, not the process.

questions.stem: It is an effect of fires delivered in a tactical mission task that results in rendering enemy personnel or materiel incapable of interfering with a particular operation and producing at least 10-percent casualties or materiel damage.
questions.explanation: Disrupt breaks up the enemy's formation, tempo and timetable. Note that the 10-percent casualty figure is normally tied to neutralization in artillery effects.
why: Destroy needs at least 30-percent casualties or damage, much more than 10 percent.
Suppress is only temporary degradation, about 3 percent casualties or damage.
Defeat means the enemy lost the physical means or will to fight, with no 10-percent measure.

questions.stem: The regulation of forces and war fighting functions to accomplish the mission in accordance with the commander's intent.
questions.explanation: Control is the regulation of forces and warfighting functions to accomplish the mission in accordance with the commander's intent.
why: Command is the authority and direction, not regulation.
Shared understanding is a Mission Command principle.
Competence is leader skill.

questions.stem: What is the uninterrupted availability of information paths for the effective performance of the C2 function?
questions.explanation: Continuity is the uninterrupted availability of information paths so command and control functions keep working.
why: Versatility is the ability to adapt to all battlefield conditions, not uninterrupted path availability.
Interoperability is the ability of units and services to communicate with each other.
Security protects information from the enemy; it is not about uninterrupted availability.

questions.stem: The assigned frequency to all aircraft engages in ISO (Internal Security Operation).
questions.explanation: 49 MHz is the frequency assigned to aircraft involved in internal security operations. Other values are different assignments.
why: 38 MHz is a different assignment and not the one set for aircraft in ISO.
52 MHz is a different assignment and not the one set for aircraft in ISO.
121.5 MHz is the international aeronautical emergency (guard) frequency, not the ISO assignment.

questions.stem: What sky wave propagation extends the range of communications between two or more stations?
questions.explanation: Of the modulation types listed, AM is the one tied to HF sky-wave work, where signals reflected by the ionosphere extend range beyond line of sight. Strictly, sky wave is a propagation path, not a modulation type; AM is keyed because HF AM is the classic sky-wave mode.
why: FM at VHF is limited to line of sight and does not rely on sky-wave reflection.
VHF is a line-of-sight band that normally passes through the ionosphere, not reflecting from it.
UHF is likewise line of sight and is not used for sky-wave range extension.

questions.stem: Detailed, unprescribed method for doing a task which can be modified or changed, as situation requires.
questions.explanation: Techniques are non-prescriptive, detailed ways of doing a task that can be changed as the situation requires.
why: Tactics is the art and science of employing and arranging combat units, not a task method.
Procedures are standard, detailed steps that are prescribed and not freely changed.
Doctrine is the authoritative guide on how the Army fights, not a flexible method.

questions.stem: During a cyber defense exercise, the team is instructed to protect critical databases from hacking attempts and prevent leakage of sensitive operational data. What component of C4S are they focusing on?
questions.explanation: Cyber systems protect networks and data from intrusion, hacking and leakage. Protecting critical databases is their focus.
why: The communications system moves information between points; it is not about defending databases.
The electronics system covers electronic equipment and emitters, not protection of data.
Electronic warfare uses the electromagnetic spectrum to attack or defend; it is not a C4S component.

questions.stem: Knowing what others perceive along with recognizing diversity and displaying self-control.
questions.explanation: Interpersonal tact is understanding how others perceive things, recognizing diversity and showing self-control in dealing with people.
why: Innovation is introducing something new, not reading and respecting others.
Warrior ethos is the will to win and do right, not social awareness.
Command responsibility is organizational accountability, not a personal interaction skill.

questions.stem: In mission analysis, which factor is NOT part of METT-TC?
questions.explanation: METT-TC stands for Mission, Enemy, Terrain and weather, Troops and support available, Time available and Civil considerations. Training is not a factor.
why: Terrain and weather is a METT-TC factor, so it is part of it.
Time available is a METT-TC factor, so it is part of it.
Civil considerations is the C of METT-TC, so it is part of it.

questions.stem: Who approves the final Operations Order at battalion/brigade level?
questions.explanation: The commander approves the final OPORD; staff officers prepare and recommend but only the commander decides.
why: The chief of staff coordinates the staff but does not approve the order.
The S3 develops operations planning and the order, but approval rests with the commander.
The S6 prepares the signal portions, not the approval of the order.

questions.stem: Which annex covers signal in an operations order?
questions.explanation: Annex H of the operations order is the signal annex; the S6 prepares it with its appendices.
why: Annex B is the intelligence annex.
Annex C is the operations annex.
Annex D is the fire support/fires annex.

questions.stem: Frequency that is assigned for Vigilance Nets.
questions.explanation: The watch frequency is the one assigned for vigilance nets, which are reserved for emergency and exigent situations and for joint operations.
why: An alternate frequency is a backup for a net, not the vigilance net assignment.
A spare frequency is a reserve and not the vigilance net assignment.
An administrative net frequency serves routine administrative traffic, not vigilance nets.

questions.stem: TLP is commonly used at which unit level?
questions.explanation: TLP is the process used by small-unit leaders, typically at platoon and company level.
why: Battalion/brigade staffs use MDMP instead.
Division and corps staffs also use MDMP.
Theater army is a very large echelon that uses staff planning, not TLP.

questions.stem: One other dimension of leadership that officers need to pay attention to.
questions.explanation: Ethics is the moral dimension of leadership that officers must attend to alongside competence.
why: Innovation is introducing something new, not a moral dimension.
Tactics is employing units in relation to each other, not a leadership dimension.
Synchronization is arranging actions in time and space, not leadership ethics.

questions.stem: It is a task clearly stated in the mission statement, operations order (OPORD), fragmentary order (FRAGO), or any formal instruction from higher command. These tasks must be accomplished as directed.
questions.explanation: A specified task is stated in the mission statement, OPORD, FRAGO or other formal instruction and must be done as directed.
why: An implied task is not stated but must be done to accomplish a specified task.
A constraint limits freedom of action rather than being a task to execute.
A course of action is a possible way to accomplish the mission, not an assigned task.

questions.stem: Consist of the principles, standards, and qualities considered essential for successful Army leaders.
questions.explanation: Army values and leader attributes (character, presence, intellect) are the principles and qualities considered essential for successful Army leaders.
why: Leader competencies are what leaders do (lead, develop, achieve), not the principles and standards.
Warfighting functions group unit tasks and are not leadership qualities.
Troop leading procedure is a planning process, not a set of values.

questions.stem: Which staff officer is primarily responsible for signal support planning at brigade?
questions.explanation: The S6 (signal staff officer) plans and manages signal support at brigade.
why: The S1 handles personnel and administration.
The S2 handles intelligence and security.
The S4 handles logistics and supply.

questions.stem: The use of weapons systems to create a specific lethal or nonlethal effect on a target?
questions.explanation: Fires is the use of weapons systems to create a specific lethal or nonlethal effect on a target.
why: Maneuver (movement and maneuver) positions forces to gain advantage.
Intelligence is gathering and analyzing information about the enemy and environment.
Sustainment provides logistics and support, not effects on targets.

questions.stem: The most essential ability of a person who leads or commands.
questions.explanation: The core leader competency, the ability to lead, develop and achieve, is the central capability of someone who leads or commands.
why: Leader attributes are character, presence and intellect, the qualities that inform competence.
Warrior ethos is the will to win, not the central competency.
Interpersonal tact is one skill within leadership, not the core competency.

questions.stem: It is the authoritative guide on how the Army fights wars and conducts operations other than war.
questions.explanation: Doctrine is the authoritative guide on how the Army fights and conducts operations, based on tested principles.
why: Tactics is employing units in relation to each other, not the guide itself.
Techniques are flexible methods of doing a task.
Warfighting functions are groups of related tasks, not the authoritative guide.

questions.stem: Is the conduct of military operations through Centralized Planning and Decentralized Execution based on commander's intent and mission orders.
questions.explanation: Mission command is conducting operations through decentralized execution based on commander's intent and mission orders. In the lesson it is the commander's way to exercise authority through trust and initiative.
why: Command and control is the exercise of authority and direction, the system, not this philosophy.
Combined arms operation integrates different arms for effect, not a command philosophy.
Synchronization is arranging actions in time and space to mass effects.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT part of the MDMP steps?
questions.explanation: The MDMP steps are receipt of mission, mission analysis, COA development, COA analysis, COA comparison, COA approval and orders production. Evaluating enemy TTPs is not a step.
why: Mission analysis is the second step of MDMP.
COA development is the third step of MDMP.
Orders production is the final step of MDMP.

questions.stem: What is the medium by which a message is conveyed from one person or place to another?
questions.explanation: A means of communications is the medium that carries a message from one person or place to another, such as wire, radio, messenger or visual.
why: An agency is a facility with people and equipment, not the medium itself.
A signal is the method or code by which information is conveyed.
A radio net is a group of stations on a common frequency.

questions.stem: The exercise of authority and direction by a properly designated commander over assigned and attached forces in the accomplishment of mission.
questions.explanation: Command and control is the exercise of authority and direction by a commander over assigned and attached forces to accomplish the mission.
why: Command responsibility is collective accountability, not the exercise of authority.
Synchronization arranges activities in time and space.
Doctrine is the guide on how the Army fights.

questions.stem: The first step in the MDMP is:
questions.explanation: The first step of MDMP is receipt of mission, when the order or warning order arrives and the staff begins preparing.
why: Mission analysis is step two.
COA development is step three.
Orders production is the last step.

questions.stem: What is a method or means of conveying information of any kind from one person or place to another?
questions.explanation: A signal is a method or means of conveying information of any kind from one person or place to another.
why: A radio net is a group of stations on a shared frequency, not the method itself.
An agency of communications is a facility with personnel and equipment.
Authentication is a way to verify legitimacy of a station or message, not the conveying method.

questions.stem: Communication links between and/or among Major Services, and the Unified Commands particularly component units of Major Services deployed within a Unified Command.
questions.explanation: Tactical communications interoperability is the set of links between and among the Services and unified commands, especially component units deployed within a unified command.
why: Strategic communications serve national-level needs, not tactical links among Services.
Administrative communications carry routine administrative traffic.
Combat net radio is a specific radio type used within units, not the interservice links.

questions.stem: Which product is the output of the MDMP process?
questions.explanation: The MDMP ends with orders production, so the order (OPORD) is its output.
why: A signal estimate is a staff analysis that feeds planning, not the final output.
An intelligence estimate is an input to planning, not its final output.
A situation template is an intelligence product used in analysis.

questions.stem: Aims at using these existing qualities and potential to develop a well-rounded leader with sets of desired attributes forming the leader's character, presence, and intellect.
questions.explanation: Military leadership attributes are the qualities that form a well-rounded leader: character, presence and intellect.
why: Competencies are what leaders do: lead, develop, achieve.
Army core values are only part of character.
Warrior Ethos is part of character.

questions.stem: An art and science involving the employment of combat units and the arrangement of maneuver units in relation to each other.
questions.explanation: Tactics is the art and science of employing combat units and arranging maneuver units in relation to each other and the enemy.
why: Techniques are non-prescriptive methods of doing a task.
Procedures are standard detailed steps.
Doctrine is the authoritative guide, not the arrangement of units.

questions.stem: How many editions is the CEOI prepared in to facilitate replacement in the event of a compromise?
questions.explanation: The exam portal keyed 2. Heads-up: the CEOI lesson's CEOI-versus-CESI comparison says the CEOI is prepared in four editions and the CESI in only one, so answer 2 for this graded item but know 4 from the lesson.
why: Only one edition would leave no ready replacement if the effective edition is compromised.
Three editions would include the second reserve, which is kept at the issuing headquarters and not issued to the unit.
Four editions would include the third reserve, which is kept only as a master copy in a storage vault.

questions.stem: Core leader competencies focus on who is being led and with what degree of authority and influence.
questions.explanation: The Leading Competency focuses on who is being led and with what authority and influence, and addresses how leaders convey influence.
why: Developing competency is about improving self, others and the organization.
Achieving competency is about accomplishing the mission.
Leaders Presence is an attribute, not a core competency.

questions.stem: Moral and ethical quality of a leader that helps determine what is right and gives a motivation to do what is appropriate.
questions.explanation: Leader character is the moral and ethical quality that determines what is right and motivates a leader to do it. It includes Army core values, empathy and Warrior Ethos.
why: Presence is the image a leader projects.
Intellect is the mental tendencies shaping conceptual abilities.
Military Leadership Attributes is the whole set that includes character, not the moral quality itself.

questions.stem: Intelligence products, organizations, and activities that incorporate all sources of information and intelligence information, including open-source information, in the production of intelligence.
questions.explanation: All-source intelligence combines products, organizations and activities that use every source, including open-source information, to produce intelligence.
why: SIGINT is limited to intercepted communications and emissions.
IMINT is limited to imagery.
HUMINT is limited to information from human sources.

questions.stem: Requires unrelenting and consistent determination to do what is right and do it with pride. It is to sustain the will to win.
questions.explanation: Warrior ethos is the unrelenting determination to do what is right with pride, sustaining the will to win and to never quit.
why: Innovation is about introducing something new.
Interpersonal tact is awareness of how others perceive things.
